readings.author: Oscar Schachter
readings.title: Dag Hammarskjold and the Relation of Law to Politics
readings.summary:
A 1962 AJIL tribute by Schachter, who worked closely with him.

**1. Law as source and basis of policy.** No sharp law/policy split (unlike positivism). Legal norms are one factor in decision, but binding and to be given priority. Charter principles proved concrete enough to resolve controversies; they embody values of most of mankind, 'a projection into the international arena … of purposes and principles already accepted as being of national validity'.

**2. Principles and flexibility.** His mind suited the interplay of norm and fact; he was impartial through principled behaviour, yet saw himself not as a judge but as a 'political technician' in crises needing ad hoc solutions. UNEF (Gaza) principles were distilled into guidelines and applied to the **Congo**: non-intervention in internal conflicts, exclusion of major powers from the force, international status, UN choice of troops, good-faith interpretation. Principles are stated as *polar opposites* (human rights vs non-intervention; equality vs great-power responsibility) to be weighed. (Schachter notes McDougal uses the same polarity.)

**3. Law and diplomacy.** A legal mandate (Security Council or Assembly) gives the conciliator *locus standi*, removing invidiousness. He built common ground on standards with a 'legal quality', implying impartiality and universality.

**4. Law, power and action.** Law grows 'organically', not as an 'ideal pattern'. He worked within bipolar power, seeking common interests (atomic energy, outer space, development), and acted in the 'power vacuums' of decolonising areas to forestall bloc intervention through aid, administration, training and even force (the Congo). This 'executive action' is part of the community's enforcement machinery and creates new standards of permissible interference.
arguments: Law and policy fused: principles as authoritative goals.
Flexible, polar application of principles to crises.
Legal mandates as diplomatic resources.
UN 'executive action' in decolonising states as new law in practice.
readings.tldr: Hammarskjöld (UN Secretary-General, died 1961) saw law not as technical rules opposed to politics but as the authoritative expression of shared goals. He applied Charter principles flexibly ('more art than engineering'), used legal mandates as diplomatic locus standi, and treated 'executive action' (UNEF, the Congo) as an organic growth of law within the limits of power.
readings.context: The Secretary-General as a hero of the 1950–89 row of [[kennedy-chart]] ('manager/statesman'). Read with Kennedy's own SG essay ([[kennedy-sg]], Topic 16), [[mcdougal-law-power]] (shared polarity method) and [[anghie-imperialism]] (the 'power vacuums' of the Third World as a new civilising terrain).

conceptNotes.law-and-politics: law as policy in UN practice

readings.author: Philip Jessup
readings.title: Transnational Law
readings.tldr: 'International' wrongly suggests only relations between states. Jessup proposes 'transnational law': 'all law which regulates actions or events that transcend national frontiers', public and private international law and rules fitting no standard category. Its actors are individuals, corporations, states, organisations and NGOs.
readings.summary:
Opening of the 1956 Storrs Lectures.
- The subject is the law of a world community from the individual up to the 'family of nations'. The national state is central but not the only group.
- 'International' and 'international law' are misleading. Scelle's *droit des gens* (law of individuals) has no English equivalent; Ross tried 'interlegal law'.
- **Definition**: 'transnational law' includes 'all law which regulates actions or events that transcend national frontiers', both public and private international law plus rules outside the standard categories. (McDougal used 'transnational' for groups, not for law.)
- **Examples**: a traveller (even stateless) whose passport is challenged at a frontier; a US oil company in Venezuela; a New York lawyer hiring French counsel for an estate; US–Soviet talks on Germany; UNICEF shipping milk; a UN mediator in Palestine; the ICC (Chamber of Commerce) at an ECOSOC conference. There are 140+ intergovernmental organisations and 1,100+ NGOs.
- Rules may conflict; choice of law may be between national laws (conflict of laws, by a national court) or between national law and public international law (by international tribunals or non-judicial decision-makers).
arguments: Replace 'international' with a broader transnational frame.
Public/private and national/international lines are artificial.
Many actors and many decision-makers.
readings.context: Grows out of Jessup's 1928 functionalism ([[jessup-functional]]). Koh builds 'transnational legal process' on it ([[koh-tlp]], Topic 13). Its public/private blending links to [[cohen-property-sovereignty]] and Topic 17's private ordering.

conceptNotes.public-private: public and private international law merged

readings.author: Ruth Wedgwood
readings.title: Unilateral Action in a Multilateral World
readings.summary:
From *Multilateralism and U.S. Foreign Policy* (2001).
- **Web of institutions**: environment, human rights, children, trade, IP, the spectrum, capital markets (informal discipline); NATO, OSCE, OAS; ad hoc groups (Contadora, 'contact groups', 'Friends of the Secretary-General'). Informality can help (COCOM, the Australia Group, the nuclear suppliers group, KEDO).
- **Why multilateralism**: coordination; binding potential spoilers; economies of scale; preventing free-riding; legitimacy (values not one country's interest); credibility of regimes.
- **Its problems**: slowness, generality masking differences, rivalries, monitoring and defection, unstable coalitions, secrecy, uneven bureaucracies, cultural misunderstanding, interoperability.
- **Force multilaterally**: joint commitments restrain arms races (NATO and Germany; US troops in Korea and Japan; 'virtual' nuclear states). Security Council or art. 51 authorisation gives legitimacy, mobilises democratic support and basing, and can police conduct (Desert Storm stopped short of Baghdad). But the UN never got art. 43 forces; it is a 'legal umbrella and political sounding board', authorising member states (Korea 1950, Gulf 1991 under US command). Alliances also manage domestic politics (Res. 678 and Congress).
- **Conclusion**: Security Council delays push the US to 'substitute' multilateralism (regional organisations, coalitions), plus consultation and public argument, which 'may cause sleepless nights for some international lawyers'. The US won't let multilateral machinery govern its force, because deterrence requires adversaries to know a response will come; otherwise blocking mechanisms could cause conflict. 'Creative ambiguity' continues.
arguments: Multilateralism is valuable but instrumentally so.
UN collective security never materialised as designed.
'Substitute multilateralism' as legitimacy without Council authorisation.
Unilateral options preserve deterrence.
readings.tldr: The US built a dense web of multilateral institutions, which coordinate, share costs, prevent free-riding and confer legitimacy. But multilateral bodies are slow, vague, hard to monitor, and the UN never worked as designed (no art. 43 forces). On force, the US often uses 'substitute multilateralism' (regional bodies, ad hoc coalitions) and keeps unilateral options, because deterrence needs credibility that a blocking veto would undermine: 'creative ambiguity'.
readings.context: A Yale/US-policy voice in 'Managing an Empire'. It sets up [[slaughter-around-un]] (2003), contrasts with [[nicaragua-1984]] (judicial control of force) and connects to Topic 22.

readings.author: Anne-Marie Slaughter
readings.title: Good Reasons for Going Around the U.N.
readings.tldr: On the eve of the 2003 Iraq invasion: giving up on the Security Council is 'illegal but legitimate', like Kosovo 1999. UN approval may come after the fact if WMD are found or Iraqis welcome the intervention and the UN is brought back to rebuild. What matters is that all sides still treat UN approval as necessary; the rules may have to evolve so that what is legitimate is also legal.
readings.summary:
NYT op-ed, 18 March 2003.
- **Kosovo precedent**: in 1999 NATO bypassed an expected Russian veto; the Independent International Commission found the intervention 'formally illegal' but 'legitimate'.
- **Iraq**: UN approval could come *after* an invasion if WMD are found, or even without them if Iraqis welcome the coalition and the US returns to the UN to rebuild. The US will claim authorisation under Res. 1441; most international lawyers will reject that; insisting on formal legality 'may be counterproductive'.
- Neither side can command a veto-free majority; both continue to claim the better argument. Importantly, everyone still treats UN approval as necessary (compare the Cold War Council sidelined, or a US invasion without any UN reference).
- The UN constrains decision-making but 'cannot be a straitjacket' on self-defence or vital security interests. Its founders built a political as well as a legal institution, wary of the 'best' being the 'enemy of the good'.
- An 'unruly process of pushing and shoving' redefines the UN's role without amendment (East Timor showed consensus is possible). 'The rules may have to evolve, so that what is legitimate is also legal.'
arguments: 'Illegal but legitimate' as a category.
Legitimacy can be retroactive and outcome-based.
UN centrality preserved as a reference point even when bypassed.
Practice changes the rules without formal amendment.
readings.context: The liberal-internationalist case for flexible legality. Compare [[wedgwood-unilateral]] (substitute multilateralism), [[koskenniemi-impunity]] (law and politics), Krever's warning about legalism ([[krever-scurrying]], Iraq 2003), and Topic 22 ([[kennedy-legal-expertise-war]]).

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: How Nations Behave: Law and Foreign Policy
readings.tldr: To many observers international law seems voluntary and hortatory, yielding to national interest. Lawyers answer that the cup is half full: law is made and grows, there is a Court, arbitration, national courts and UN organs, and horizontal enforcement. Above all, critics ask the wrong questions. What matters is whether law is *observed* and shapes behaviour, and it largely is.
readings.summary:
From *How Nations Behave* (2nd ed. 1979), pp. 25–26.
- **The sceptic's view**: governments seem free to agree to new law, to accept others' views, and to comply or not. International law is 'voluntary and only hortatory' and must yield to national interest (security, power, prestige). Diplomats think it unrealistic to build policy on it and are impatient with their lawyers.
- **Lawyers' reply**: admit the limits but deny their implications; reject Austin's definition; law grows even if slowly; the ICJ's few judgments are respected; arbitration fills gaps; national courts develop the law; Security Council and General Assembly actions interpret and develop law and deter; there is 'horizontal enforcement' by other nations' reactions.
- **The right question**: not whether there are legislative, judicial and executive branches like a domestic system, but 'whether international law is reflected in the policies of nations'. Not whether law is enforced but 'whether law is observed, whether it governs or influences behavior'. 'Nations have accepted important limitations on their sovereignty', observed them, and the result is 'substantial order'.
- *(The famous line, 'almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law and almost all of their obligations almost all of the time', comes later in the book and is not in this excerpt.)*
arguments: Shift from enforcement to compliance as the test of law.
Institutional gaps are partly filled by other mechanisms.
Observance, not structure, makes international law real.
readings.context: 'Back to norms and values' after the policy-science moment ([[mcdougal-law-power]]); answers [[austin-province]] differently from [[kelsen-lecture-iii]] (behaviour, not sanction). Koh builds on it ([[koh-tlp]]).

conceptNotes.compliance: observance as the measure of law

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: International Law and the Inter-State System
readings.summary:
From *International Law: Politics and Values* (1995), Part I.
- Any legal system reflects its political system; international law reflects an inter-state system.
- *Law is politics*: the law/politics distinction is 'only a part-truth'. Law is the resultant of political forces, and its influence on behaviour is politically determined. But law isn't depreciated: it 'permeates, supports and maintains' the system and shapes how nations behave; lawyers, courts, publicists and bodies like the Institut and the ALI enrich or impoverish it.
- Domestic law expresses a domestic society of people (and juristic persons) and serves order, reliable expectations, protection of persons and property, welfare and justice.
- International law analogously serves order, expectations, protection of 'persons' and values, but its constituency is *states*: an inter-state system.
arguments: Law and politics are intertwined, not opposed.
International law mirrors a state-centred political system.
The domestic analogy is useful with caution.
readings.tldr: 'Law is politics': made by political actors, through political procedures, for political ends. But law also permeates and shapes the political system. International law is the normative expression of an *inter-state* system whose 'persons' are states, not human beings, with purposes (order, reliable expectations, protection, values) analogous to domestic law.
readings.context: Mainstream liberal statism in 1995, the counterpoint to Jessup's transnationalism ([[jessup-transnational]]) and Kennedy's critique of the state-centred frame. Compare Álvarez ('pure law does not exist', [[corfu-1949-merits]]) and McDougal ([[mcdougal-law-power]]).

readings.author: Harold H. Koh
readings.title: Transnational Legal Process
readings.tldr: Transnational legal process is how public and private actors interact across fora to make, interpret, enforce and *internalise* international law. It is nontraditional, nonstatist, dynamic and normative. Henkin said nations mostly comply; Koh explains *why*: not interest alone, nor liberal identity, but repeated *interaction → interpretation → internalisation* that makes law 'sticky'.
readings.summary:
1994 Roscoe Pound Lecture (Nebraska L. Rev. 1996).

**Definition.** 'How public and private actors (nation-states, international organizations, multinational enterprises, NGOs and private individuals) interact in a variety of public and private, domestic and international fora to make, interpret, enforce, and ultimately, internalize rules of transnational law.' Four features: *nontraditional* (breaks domestic/international and public/private), *nonstatist*, *dynamic* (law percolates up and down), and *normative* (new rules emerge and guide future conduct).

**Example: Dames & Moore.** A private nuclear site-study contract with Iran's Atomic Energy Organization became, through the 1979 revolution and hostage crisis, a public dispute: Iranian expropriations, US sanctions and asset freezes, the Algiers executive agreement transferring claims to the Iran–US Claims Tribunal, a Supreme Court loss (*Dames & Moore v. Regan*), and a Tribunal case. It was 'jurisgenerative' (Cover), generating new domestic and international law.

**Why nations obey.** Henkin: almost all nations observe almost all law almost all the time. But why?
- *Interest* (rationalist, game theory, regimes): compliance serves long-term self-interest in repeated games; law reduces transaction costs and signals defection.
- *Identity* (Slaughter's liberal theory): liberal states form a 'zone of law', illiberal ones a 'zone of politics'. But identity isn't fixed: states move between dictatorship and democracy (Argentina, Chile, Peru, Haiti), prodded by international law.
- *Interaction and internalisation*: violations create frictions in ongoing participation (*Alvarez-Machain* kidnapping hurt NAFTA talks; sovereign default hurts lending; denying ICJ jurisdiction as defendant hurts you as plaintiff). Repeated interaction produces norms that are internalised through executive action, legislation and judicial decisions; decision-making becomes 'enmeshed'. That is how law gets its 'stickiness' and states come to define compliance as in their interest. (Analogy: seat-belt rules internalised by drivers.) Even 'rogue states' must eventually interact. A violator may instead push to reinterpret the norm, which triggers another round of contestation.

**Conclusions.** The theory predicts compliance if transnational processes are aggressively triggered; it suits lawyers' comparative advantage; it calls for *clinical* work and 'transnational public law litigation' to create frictions (a lawyer who understands the body politic, like a doctor, has a duty to act); and it fills 'the hole in the doughnut': scholars have been doing transnational legal process 'without knowing it', like Molière's prose.
arguments: Compliance is produced by interaction and internalisation, not just coercion or interest.
Identity is constructed through legal process, not given.
Breaking public/private and domestic/international divides.
Normative activism: lawyers should trigger the process (litigation, advocacy).
readings.context: Built on [[henkin-how-nations-behave]] and [[jessup-transnational]]; a 1990s 'citizen/NGO advocate and national judge' figure of [[kennedy-chart]]. Applied in [[koh-trump]], questioned by [[goldsmith-mercer]] and [[hakimi-cogan]]. Compare [[paquete-habana]] and [[techt-v-hughes]] (reception in national courts).

conceptNotes.reception: internalisation through domestic courts and legislatures

readings.author: Harold H. Koh
readings.title: The Trump Administration and International Law
readings.tldr: Transnational legal process as 'rope-a-dope'. Outsiders (NGOs, litigants, states, cities) use *interaction–interpretation–internalisation*; insiders (bureaucrats) use *engage–translate–leverage* ('international law as smart power'). Together they create default compliance that makes Trump's 'disengage–black hole–hard power' costly, so he may 'move on'. At stake: a Kantian order of cooperation vs Orwellian spheres of influence.
readings.summary:
2017 Foulston Siefkin Lecture, nine months into Trump's first term, by a former State Department Legal Adviser.

**Core insight.** Most compliance comes from 'patterns of obedience' and internalised norms, not coercion: 'Even all alone at 2 o'clock in the morning, most of us still stop for a red light.'

**Two strategies.**
- *Outside*: NGOs and others generate interactions (lawsuits) that force interpretations (rulings) the government must internalise (obey).
- *Inside*: 'Engage–Translate–Leverage', the 'Obama–Clinton doctrine' and Clinton's 'smart power'. Choose engagement over unilateralism. Choose good-faith *translation* of the spirit of existing law to new situations (drones, cyber) over the 'Tina Turner question' ('What's law got to do with it?') and claims of a 'legal black hole'. Leverage law with other tools (Dayton, New START, Paris).
- Together they produce 'default compliance' that makes casual deviation hard.

**Trump's counter-philosophy.** 'Disengage–black hole–hard power': 'America First', national rather than universal rights, no diplomatic strategy. Who will change whom? No single player can easily discard the rules. If exit is costly, a mercurial president may 'check the box' and move on. Outside actors and states and localities can resist; bureaucrats maintain default compliance unless explicitly ordered otherwise. (Case studies in the table of contents: immigration and refugees, human rights, climate, Iran, North Korea, Russian hacking, Ukraine, Al Qaeda/IS, Syria.)

**At stake.** A Kantian system of global governance (UN, WTO, Paris, the Iran deal, with the US as 'balance wheel') vs a cynical Orwellian world of authoritarian mega-powers, disinformation and spheres of influence. Early signs give reason for optimism: 'the game is on, and the stakes are high.'
arguments: Resistance through law: litigation and bureaucratic inertia constrain a hostile executive.
'Translation' rather than legal black holes for new technologies.
Default compliance and path dependence make exit costly.
Framed as a civilisational choice: Kant vs Orwell.
readings.context: Applies [[koh-tlp]]; the target of [[goldsmith-mercer]]'s scepticism and Benvenisti's 'third response' ([[benvenisti-resilience]]). Compare [[bolton-icc-2018]] (the administration's own voice) and [[kennedy-legal-expertise-war]] (law as the vocabulary of power, not just its constraint).

readings.author: Jack Goldsmith & Shannon Togawa Mercer
readings.title: International Law and Institutions in the Trump Era
readings.summary:
Draft for the German Yearbook of International Law (2019).

**Part I (the 'onslaught').** Trump treats international law and institutions with disdain ('independence and cooperation over global governance' at the UN), with withdrawals and threats.

**Comparison with Bush.** Bush also withdrew (ABM Treaty, the consular-relations protocol) and ended his presidency with ratings similar to Trump's after two years. Obama was seen as restorer, though he couldn't undo everything (Guantánamo, Iraq). So one presidency's impact is hard to predict, and institutions can survive long US disengagement. Koh argues Trump's effects can be limited.

**The bigger picture.**
- *Baseline problem*: the US-led order was neither as rule-based, orderly nor normatively attractive as critics claim. It didn't prevent Syria, Iraq, Libya, Yemen, Crimea, Georgia or the South China Sea; the WTO was seen as ossified and distributively unfair; democracy had declined for twelve years running (Freedom House); the populist revolt, Brexit and Obama's 'leading from behind' (Kagan: 'America First' is a pithier 'nation-building at home') came first.
- *Causation problem*: China's and Russia's rise, backlash against globalising institutions, war fatigue and disenchantment with elite institutions predate Trump, who 'might be mostly … epiphenomenal'.
- So Koh is wrong that a *snap-back* to 2016 is possible. China now leads on climate and trade (AIIB, New Development Bank); power shifts are path-dependent.
- *Trump's unique contribution*: rhetoric. Calling the UN, NATO, EU, WTO, human rights bodies and G-7 corrupt and harmful corrodes faith, emboldens other populists, invites retaliation, and dislodges 'the consensus whiggish belief in a one-directional, ever-deepening, ever-more-progressive international order'.
- Kissinger: Trump may be one of those figures 'who appears from time to time to mark the end of an era … It could just be an accident.'
arguments: Measure change against a realistic baseline, not an idealised 'liberal order'.
Structural forces, not one president, drive change.
No snap-back: path dependence and power shifts.
Words matter: rhetorical delegitimation is Trump's distinctive impact.
readings.tldr: Trump's attacks on international law and institutions are real, but it is too early to measure their impact. The 'rules-based order' was never as rule-based or attractive as claimed. Structural forces (China, Russia, the populist backlash, overstretch) predate him, so he may be 'epiphenomenal'. A Koh-style snap-back is unlikely. His distinctive harm is probably *rhetorical*: delegitimising institutions and the Whig belief in ever-progressive international law.
readings.context: A realist corrective to [[koh-trump]], from the Bush-era OLC veteran. Read with [[hakimi-cogan]] (co-constitution of law and US power) and [[benvenisti-resilience]] (empire and jus cogens). Compare the 'Whig' narratives critiqued in [[kennedy-chart]] and [[damrosch-intro]].

readings.author: Eyal Benvenisti
readings.title: The Resilience of International Law in the Face of Empire
readings.summary:
Just Security, 17 February 2025.
- **Trends**: early second-term proposals sidestep sovereignty and human rights. We may be reverting 'to an era of imperial rule'. Not solely Trump's doing (Russia and China); but there is a difference between *invoking* law for partisan ends (Putin's misapplied self-defence still reinforces the law, as *Nicaragua* 1986 noted) and *disavowing* it, which rejects sovereign equality and accountability.
- **Territorial entrenchment** (Brunk & Hakimi): the triad of sanctity of borders, prohibition of force and self-determination; the ban on forcible annexation is jus cogens. It crystallised in 1945, matured through decolonisation, and gained enforcement when a US-dominated Security Council acted in the 1990s, which fostered globalisation, trust and falling military spending (1990–98). Then erosion: Kosovo, Iraq, the South China Sea, Georgia, Crimea; China–Russia vetoes since 2011; rising military spending since 1998 (sharply since 2014). A 'new era of colonial domination' by three nuclear powers may loom.
- **ICJ 2024 Advisory Opinion (OPT)**: territorial sovereignty is not subject to external challenge; permanent control without consent is annexation and unlawful; the 'law of occupation' (not just belligerent) limits foreign control.
- **Responses**: (1) collective state action (erga omnes duties of non-recognition and non-assistance; broad condemnation of Russia, which may fade under Trump); (2) institutional (the ICJ extends non-recognition to IOs including the UN, but the P5 are split); (3) transnational legal process (Koh), which needs resilient democracies; (4) *documentation*: international law 'hibernates' and 'has a long memory'. The Baltic republics regained sovereignty after fifty years. Unless a new peremptory norm is accepted by a 'very large and representative majority' (ILC), jus cogens stays valid.
arguments: Disavowal of law is worse than manipulation of it.
Territorial entrenchment is the core of post-1945 law and is jus cogens.
Enforcement depends on power alignments that have broken down.
Law persists through memory and documentation even in an 'age of empire'.
readings.tldr: Trump's second term (Gaza 'evacuation', accepting Russia's hold on Ukraine, not ruling out force for Greenland or Panama) disavows rather than manipulates international law, which is more sinister since it rejects accountability itself. The post-1945 'territorial entrenchment' (borders, no force, self-determination) is jus cogens. When enforcement fails, law 'hibernates': lawyers and historians must document it until order returns, as with the Baltic states.
readings.context: Bridges Topic 8 ([[vidmar-greenland]], [[western-sahara]]) and Topic 3 ([[ilc-fragmentation-jus-cogens]]) with the Topic 13 debate on [[koh-trump]] and [[hakimi-cogan]]. Its 'colonial domination' worry links to Topic 19 ([[anghie-postcolonial]]).

readings.author: Monica Hakimi & Jacob Katz Cogan
readings.title: The End of the U.S.-Backed International Order and the Future of International Law
readings.summary:
AJIL 2025.
- **Change**: the US-led order (trade, statehood, democracy, human rights, multilateralism, institutions), with heterogeneous global origins but the US as principal guarantor, is undergoing dramatic change.
- **Law and power**: law needs power to be effective, and power uses law, but 'law's primary allegiance is to its own processes and rules, not the preferences of the powerful'. If power's demands become excessive, law resists. Alignment is imperfect, impermanent and contingent. A breakdown can be a blip or an order's dissolution.
- **Four features of the US-backed system**: (1) *legalisation*: law as a dominant mode of interaction, a flourishing of courts and treaties, with the US drafting and advancing the WTO, Rome Statute, Paris and model bilateral agreements; (2) *institutions*; (3) *support for states as states* (statehood, territorial integrity); (4) *extensive regulation of states* (human rights, trade, anti-corruption, investment, health, Antarctica).
- **Not neutral**: the US promoted law for its own goals (global health protecting US security and pharma; trade and investment favouring the US) and undermined other norms: expansive self-defence, Iraq 2003, defying the ICJ, not joining treaties, undercutting the ICC. Yet its support was 'extraordinary' and constitutive.
- **Going forward**: a less US-dominated order has appeal. US dominance reproduced colonial economic injustice via transnational capitalism, caused suffering (Iraq; sanctions on Cuba and Iran; backed dictators), and cost Americans (half of discretionary spending on the military; decisions without democratic debate). But international lawyers have failed to see how law and US power were constituted together. New, possibly illiberal, sources of power will define what law becomes; all four features are under strain; 'nothing … including the legalization of international relations itself, is guaranteed.' Think creatively about what comes next.
arguments: International law and US hegemony were co-constituted, not simply opposed.
The US-backed order = legalisation + institutions + state support + state regulation.
US support was selective and self-serving but foundational.
As power shifts, the form and content of international law will change, possibly radically.
readings.tldr: International law and US power were *co-constituted* after 1945. The US-backed order had four features: deep legalisation, commitment to institutions, support for states as states, and extensive regulation of states. US support was partial and self-interested, but foundational. As US backing ends, international law's architecture and content will change; lawyers who see power only as law's corrupter miss this.
readings.context: The structural counterpart to [[goldsmith-mercer]] and the opposite of law-as-autonomous-resistance in [[koh-trump]]. It resonates with [[mcdougal-law-power]] (law within the power process), [[kennedy-chart]] (eras shaped by power) and TWAIL critiques ([[chimni-2017]], [[anghie-imperialism]]).

readings.author: Wilhelm Röpke
readings.title: Economic Order and International Law
readings.tldr: International trade rests ultimately not on comparative costs but on *pacta sunt servanda*. The 19th-century liberal order solved the absence of a world state with an 'as-if world state': a secularised Res Publica Christiana plus Pax Britannica, the gold standard, and above all the *separation of Imperium from Dominium* (depoliticising the economy). The welfare state and collectivism re-fused them and 'nationalised man'. The cure is to *reduce* sovereignty, not transfer planning to a European super-state.
readings.summary:
Hague Academy lectures (1955) by the German ordoliberal economist.

**The problem.** Intensive division of labour requires a moral, legal and institutional framework that protects exchange: a stable, free currency and a reliable legal order plus an unwritten code of conduct. Domestically the state supplies these. Internationally there is no world state, so no world law or money. How, then, did the 19th century achieve a world economy differing from national economies only in degree?

**The liberal solution.**
1. *International 'open society'* (Bergson): a secularised, globalised Res Publica Christiana, an *ordre public international* respected with an 'air of sanctity'. Violations came 'with a bad conscience', not 'grinning cynicism'. Long-term treaties, balance of power protecting small states, and uniform legal concepts. Realistically it also needed a dominant power: Great Britain and London as centre (Pax Britannica). Will the US take its place?
2. *Separation of Imperium and Dominium* (Hume, Smith; MacIver's political vs economic power): economic life moved from the sphere of the state (public law, administration) to society (market, private law, property). This minimised the economic significance of borders. Gold standard: an 'as-if world money' produced by national currency laws plus loyalty to the 'rules of the game', with no international authority. 'An economic but not a political currency system', whose base was ultimately moral.
3. *For international law*: traditional international law is the legal side of this liberal order, especially in its treatment of **private property**, kept independent of sovereignty and nationality. Free access to raw materials made colonial possession 'anachronistic'. 'Political power has determinate frontiers, economic power has the freedom of the world.'

**Disintegration.** The interventionist welfare state, trade unions and fiscalism produce the 'nationalisation of man': 'social' means 'national' (social insurance makes the passport an insurance policy). Exchange control is the 'nationalisation of insolvency'. Borders become lines dividing different, politically manipulable conditions; devaluations rewrite thousands of contracts overnight; arbitrariness replaces order. *Collectivism* completes this: the plan replaces the price mechanism, sovereignty is raised 'to the n-th power', and planning requires national autarky.

**International planning?** The 'paradox of national collectivism' leads socialists to propose European planning, but that needs a collectivist European super-state, which is utopian and dangerous. Two meanings of sovereignty: *external* independence and *internal* supremacy over citizens (Hobbes's Leviathan). The real problem is *excessive* internal sovereignty. Don't shift its seat; reduce its *measure*: leave the economy to the 'sovereignty of the market'.
arguments: The world economy rests on a legal-moral order, ultimately pacta sunt servanda.
The liberal order = an as-if world state: open society + hegemon + gold standard.
Key principle: separate Imperium (state) from Dominium (market/property).
Welfare and collectivism re-politicise the economy, causing international disintegration.
Reduce sovereignty's measure rather than move it to supranational planners.
readings.context: The ordoliberal blueprint behind postwar economic law (European integration, GATT). It is the exact opposite of [[cohen-property-sovereignty]], which shows Dominium *is* Imperium. Continue to [[bello-wto]], [[danielsen-corporate]], [[koskenniemi-laws-rule-us]] and Topic 19's NIEO ([[bedjaoui-nieo]]), which attacks this order.

readings.author: Judith Bello
readings.title: The WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding: Less is More
readings.tldr: Critics say WTO dispute settlement lets 'faceless bureaucrats in Geneva' usurp US sovereignty. But WTO rules are not 'binding' in the traditional sense: a losing member may comply, compensate, or accept retaliation. The only sacred duty is to maintain the negotiated *balance of concessions*. This flexibility preserves sovereignty and democratic accountability and exposes the price of protectionism: 'less is more'.
readings.summary:
AJIL editorial comment (1996) by a former USTR General Counsel.
- **Backlash**: environmental groups were angered by GATT tuna–dolphin rulings (US primary and secondary boycotts inconsistent with GATT); US states by rulings on discriminatory alcohol taxes; economic nationalists (Buchanan, Perot) by 'faceless, unelected, unaccountable bureaucrats in Geneva'.
- **Not binding in the traditional sense**: 'The WTO has no jailhouse, no bail bondsmen, no blue helmets, no truncheons or tear gas.' It is a confederation of sovereign governments relying on voluntary compliance.
- **Built-in flexibility**: GATT art. II tariff bindings could be renegotiated (art. XXVIII) if compensation restored the overall balance. The only inviolable thing is 'the overall balance of rights and obligations'.
- **Three choices** after an adverse ruling: comply; keep the measure and pay compensation; or neither, and suffer authorised retaliation.
- **Why comply anyway**: reciprocity, credibility, avoiding compensation or retaliation costs, and protecting cooperation on other issues (drugs, migration, arms control, environment, rights).
- **Real reason for complaints**: the system 'sheds light on the costs' of protectionism and of using trade for non-trade objectives. Special interests prefer those costs hidden.
- 'The less binding the individual rules … the more the WTO accommodates the demands of national sovereignty … With respect to WTO dispute settlement, less is generally more.'
arguments: WTO obligations function as priced options, not absolute duties.
Balance of concessions is the only true obligation.
Sovereignty and democratic accountability are preserved by flexibility.
Transparency about protectionism's costs is the system's real effect.
Non-trade objectives (environment, labour) are disciplined by price.
readings.context: A mid-1990s trade lawyer's defence of the WTO. It is a version of the law/non-law boundary ([[schachter-twilight]]; [[nuclear-tests]]) and of Röpke's depoliticised economic order ([[roepke-1955]]). Critiques: [[shalakany-arbitration]] (Third World), [[danielsen-local-rules]] and [[iglp-gvc]] (distributional effects). Compare the 1990–2000 row of [[kennedy-chart]] (trade and economic management).

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Foundations of Human Rights in Law
readings.summary:
**What is in the packet.** Page 886 of the casebook, i.e. the end of Ch. 12 on immunity. It covers the administrative tribunals of international organisations (the ILO Tribunal, serving about 45 organisations; the UN Administrative Tribunal; the ICJ's 1954 advisory opinion that the General Assembly could not refuse to honour its awards). The right-hand column, which opens Ch. 13 on human rights, is truncated in the scan. Its visible fragments sketch the usual postwar story: the Second World War as a turning point; human rights pursued through national and international institutions; regional systems (Europe, the Americas); Cold War constraints; and a later focus on violations and institutions.

**How to use it.** As the doctrinal 'official story' against which the rest of the topic is read. Human rights is treated as a post-1945 body of treaty and custom, built out through institutions. Damrosch's next section ([[damrosch-competing]]) lays out the tensions inside that story.
arguments: Doctrinal frame: human rights as a post-1945 body of law and institutions.
(Packet scan is incomplete; check the casebook for the full section.)
readings.tldr: Casebook opening to the human rights chapter. The packet scan is only partial: the page reproduced is mostly the end of the immunity chapter (international organisations' administrative tribunals), and the human rights column is cut off. Use it as a framing device only.

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Competing Interests
readings.summary:
Casebook text (Ch. 13 §B).
1. **Individual vs state.** Human dignity, protected by civil, political and even economic rights, against the state's need to keep law and order (arrest, incarceration, punishment, prohibiting dangerous speech). Economic rights (work, education, shelter) also run up against the scarce resources of many states.
2. **Allocation of governmental authority.** Human rights live in treaty and custom handled by foreign ministries. In federal systems such as the US, however, rights questions (privacy, due process, safety) sit at lower levels of government. The field must work 'without trampling on the constitutional structures of states'. Some states (again the US) regard their domestic systems as sufficient and see little need to incorporate international human rights.
3. **Universalism vs cultural pluralism.** At its strongest, relativism denies any transcendent values that all states could agree on, which challenges the movement's founding premise. Universalists answer that some rights (not to be arbitrarily killed) cannot differ between societies. They add that the community shares an interest in common standards by which states judge one another, and in mechanisms of implementation and compliance.

**Illustration.** Recurring disputes over bans on Islamic headscarves or full-face veils pit religious freedom against public order. The packet ends as the case is introduced.
arguments: Rights vs order and resources.
International norms vs federal and domestic constitutional structure.
Universal standards vs cultural difference.
Headscarf and veil bans as the test case for all three.
readings.tldr: Human rights has to balance three sets of tensions. (1) The individual versus the state's need for order and its limited resources. (2) International obligations versus domestic and federal allocations of authority. (3) Universalism versus cultural pluralism or relativism. Bans on headscarves and veils illustrate all three.
readings.context: The textbook map of tensions inside the field. [[kennedy-hr-problem]] goes further: these 'balances' are where the movement's costs hide (centring the state, the universal vs the local). Universalism vs relativism connects to the [[becker-lorca-mestizo]] debate over who universal law belongs to. The federalism point echoes [[koh-tlp]] (domestic internalisation).

readings.author: Walter Johnson
readings.title: To Remake the World: Slavery, Racial Capitalism, and Justice
readings.tldr: Saying slavery 'dehumanized' enslaved people is misleading and harmful. Slavery depended on their *human* capacities: labour, reproduction, sentience, intelligence, fear. The frame lets latter-day observers separate a normative 'humanity' from the violence humans actually commit, and makes black humanity 'probationary'. Celebrating slaves' 'agency' anachronistically recasts them as liberal subjects. Marx's critique of abstract rights-based emancipation applies.
readings.summary:
Boston Review forum essay (pp. 15–17 in the packet).

**Misleading.** Slavery 'depended upon the human capacities of enslaved people': their reproduction, their labour, their sentience. They could be taught, manipulated, terrorised and tortured. The most 'inhuman' acts (torture, rape, humiliation) depended on violated slaves bearing witness, providing a 'living, human register of slaveholders' power'. Calling such acts 'inhuman' separates a normative, aspirational idea of humanity from forms of exploitation and violence that history suggests may well be *definitive* of human beings. 'We are separating ourselves from our own histories of perpetration.'

**Harmful.** 'Dehumanization' implies that enslaved people were alienated from their humanity. Who decides when humanity is lost, or regained? These paternalist questions lock the frame 'in an inextricable embrace with the very history of racial abjection it ostensibly confronts', while asserting the 'humanity' of the observer.

**Agency.** Historians who 'prove' black humanity (Philip Morgan, *Slave Counterpoint*) render it 'intellectually probationary'. Treating 'independent will and volition' as proof of humanity reduces everything enslaved people did (singing a spiritual, breaking a tool, revolution, a better sluiceway) to one anachronistic liberal moral: agency proved humanity. Enslaved people become would-be bourgeois rights-bearers.

**Marx.** The tension resembles the one Marx saw in 'On the Jewish Question' between material inequality and abstract rights-based equality. The citizen is 'an imaginary member of an imaginary universality'. Political emancipation is 'a big step forward', but not 'real, practical emancipation'.
arguments: Slavery exploited humanity rather than erasing it.
'Dehumanization' flatters observers and distances present from past perpetration.
Proving enslaved humanity makes that humanity probationary.
'Agency' imposes a liberal-subject template on enslaved people.
Rights-based emancipation is abstract (Marx): political, not real, emancipation.
readings.context: A historian's version of [[kennedy-hr-problem]]'s worry that human rights generalises too much and makes 'victims'. With [[nesiah-slavery-afterlives]]: both show how condemning slavery as 'inhuman' can sanitise the political economy that continues it. Racial capitalism connects to [[anghie-imperialism]] and the political-economy theme ([[roepke-1955]], [[cohen-property-sovereignty]]).

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: The International Human Rights Movement: Part of the Problem?
readings.tldr: A pragmatic checklist of the human rights movement's possible costs, not a general critique. It occupies the field of emancipation, views problems too narrowly (state, form, background), generalises and particularises too much, is tied to Western liberalism, promises more than it can deliver, legitimates violations, professionalises and demobilises, and strengthens bad global governance. Whether any cost materialises depends on context. The real question today is how *good* people go wrong.
readings.summary:
Ch. 1 of *The Dark Sides of Virtue* (2004).

**Method.** The movement has done great good. This is a *pragmatic* list of hypotheses about costs, to be weighed case by case. Kennedy counts something as a cost only if it has a bad effect. He sets aside whether rights 'really exist', whether they reflect consensus or are coherent, and complaints that could be fixed by more commitment (more enforcement, more rights). 'Benefits' are really *distributions* toward those who share humanitarian aims. Costs are usually stated generally; benefits locally. Example: a pro bono campaign against the Caribbean death penalty may look different from London and from the Caribbean.

**The list.**
1. **Occupies the field of emancipatory possibility.** Hegemony as resource allocation, as criticism (others look 'too political'), and as distortion: projects must be framed as rights to be heard. Duty-based or collective vocabularies are lost; 'right to a clean environment' vs a duty to work for it. The *right to development* draws energy into impossible questions (whose right? against whom?) while neoliberals take over development policy.
2. **Too narrow.** It foregrounds harms by the state and public remedies, and legitimates private harms. It *insulates the economy*: participation and procedure over distribution. 'That's my right' extracts from the state, not the economy, unless you own property. It *foregrounds form*: rules and machinery become ends, like elections replacing engagement. 'Is the right to vote a floor — or … a ceiling?' It *backgrounds the background*: the laws that actually shape the incidence of abuse (e.g. neutral religious freedom in Africa favouring evangelical sects).
3. **Generalises too much.** An abstract person and 'group'; becoming free 'only as an instance of the general' (alienation); answers rather than questions. A theatre of victims, violators and bystanders: 'uncivilized deviants, baby seals, and knights errant'. Bad for advocates too (sanctimony, arrogant earnestness).
4. **Particularises too much.** Bounded right-holding identities blunt solidarity and community. It *strengthens the state*: freedom becomes having an appropriately organised state. Rights are trumps, 'queue jumping'. That blocks distributive bargaining and leaves triage to the state. Certifying 'refugees' cuts them off from origin and destination; the stillborn 'right to asylum'.
5. **Western liberalism.** Origins matter pragmatically only if they bring costs. Here they bring the downsides of the West (secularism) and its pairs (economy before politics before law, private before public). Emancipation is sought in law over politics, reason over faith. In 'the West and the Rest', human rights runs one way, from centre to periphery. It exports absolute property rights unknown in the West, and frames politics as tradition vs modernity, which strengthens 'traditionalists'.
6. **Promises more than it can deliver.** Knowledge (justice found, not made). Justice outside politics: rights conflict and are vague, and the judge is fetishised. Community (the first-world media audience as the 'international community', 'an astonishing act of disenfranchisement'). Neutral intervention. The emancipator mistaken for emancipation: work on the field mistaken for work on the problem (rights → remedies → basic needs → enforcement, shifts that reflect elite fashion).
7. **Produces and excuses more violations than it prevents.** It treats symptoms. Humanitarian norms *excuse* too much (like the laws of war) and *justify* too much: the US, UK, Russia, Serbia and the Kosovars all invoked human rights. Background norms (sovereignty, property, contract, agency) do the real damage, e.g. facilitating torture.
8. **The bureaucracy is part of the problem.** It professionalises the humanitarian impulse (lawyers over 'priests, engineers, politicians, soothsayers'; East Timor elites turning 'like sunflowers to Geneva'). It degrades legal craft and serves as a fig leaf for the commercial bar. It produces false solidarity and *bad faith*: redescribing torture as 'public health'. 'Speaking law to politics is not the same thing as speaking truth to power.' Performances aimed at an 'imaginary third eye'. The perils of representation: producing authentic victims is 'voyeuristic or pornographic'. Irresponsible, unaccountable discretion.
9. **Strengthens bad international governance.** The weakest link: rules and institutions over the standards and private-law models that work better in environmental and economic law. Clean hands: intervening without responsibility for distribution. Fantasy government: legal, not political. Governing the exception: treating the tips of icebergs entrenches the rest. Denouncing sovereignty attests to its continuity.
10. **Bad politics in particular contexts.** It can strengthen repressive states (and the IFIs' structural adjustment). It can be captured, as when the 1998 'responsibilities' declaration served privatisation. *Condemnation as legitimation*: calling Bosnia a 'human rights violation' and sending lawyers can be 'a way of doing nothing'. Renaming Auschwitz 'genocide' can be a way of 'unthinking its everyday reality'.

**Close.** The founding generation asked how evil people could be restrained. Now the question is 'how good people, well-intentioned people in good societies, can go wrong'. Don't treat the movement 'as a frail child'.
arguments: Assess human rights pragmatically: costs and benefits in context, as distributions.
It crowds out other emancipatory vocabularies and insulates the economy.
Form, the state and 'victims/violators/bystanders' narrow the imagination.
Background rules (property, sovereignty, contract) do the real damage.
The professional bureaucracy breeds bad faith, voyeurism and unaccountable discretion.
Naming atrocity a 'violation' can legitimate and normalise it.
readings.short: Kennedy — HR: part of the problem?
readings.context: Kennedy's signature 'dark sides' move, the culmination of [[kennedy-chart]] and [[kennedy-primitive]]. 'Background norms' recalls [[cohen-property-sovereignty]] and [[danielsen-local-rules]]. Condemnation as legitimation parallels [[koskenniemi-impunity]], [[engle-grip]] and [[drumbl-smouldering]] on criminal law. Insulating the economy pairs with [[roepke-1955]]'s Imperium/Dominium split. Lived from the inside in [[kennedy-spring-break]]; historicised in [[nesiah-slavery-afterlives]] and [[johnson-slavery]].

readings.author: Vasuki Nesiah
readings.title: Slavery's Afterlives: Humanitarian Imperialism and Free Contract
readings.summary:
AJIL Unbound symposium on race and international law (2023).

**Setting.** The Slavery Abolition Act (1833) affected about 800,000 people. Scholars speak of the 'tyranny of the Atlantic'. In the Indian Ocean, abolition caused a labour crisis that was met by indenture: 2.2 million people moved across oceans over a century. Mauritius sugar was the 'petri dish'; workers came mostly from India and went to Mauritius, Réunion, Ceylon, Africa and the Caribbean. The Royal Navy policed the seas for abolition while the 'commercial twin', the indenture ships, used the same maritime infrastructure.

**Civilisational capital.** Abolition let Britain recast empire as protection. Humanitarian virtue accrued 'racialized credit'. India was exempted until 1843 so local elites could be morally 'tutored'. Slavery became a marker of the civilisational deficits of the colonised. Mussolini abolished slavery as one of his first acts in occupied Ethiopia (1935). This rhymes with Mutua's Savages–Victims–Saviors triad.

**Protection + free contract.** The slavery analogy defined coercion as physical capture, not structural impoverishment. Colonial taxes, commercialised crops and exclusion from property drove debt bondage. The Workman's Breach of Contract Act (1859) and the Penal Code (1860) criminalised breach. Debts became hereditary; servitude was run by ledgers rather than whips. Officials distinguished debt-bonded people from 'true' slaves. The injustices of indenture became a *welfare* problem (better ships, labour market formalisation) for an enlightened colonial authority. Spectacular physical violence was foregrounded while poverty was naturalised 'as much a part of the landscape as the monsoons'. Recruits came largely from oppressed castes, some from so-called 'slave castes'. Penal sanctions gave slavery 'a new lease of life within the formal terms of abolition', as in the post-emancipation US.

**Conclusion.** The slavery/freedom binary supplanted distributive analysis of indenture and wage labour. Invoking slavery 'served to distract from, disguise, and even defend atrocity'. It married 'the moral promise of protection and the economic profit from precarity', and constrained the imagination of future freedoms. 'There was much more to lose than chains.'
arguments: Abolition was reframed as imperial humanitarian virtue ('civilizational capital').
The slavery analogy defined coercion as physical, naturalising economic coercion.
Indenture and wage labour were legitimated as free contract plus protection.
Imperialism, humanitarianism and capitalism are elective affinities.
The slavery/freedom binary displaced distributive analysis.
readings.tldr: After British abolition (1833), slavery was replaced in the Indian Ocean world by indenture (2.2 million workers). Invoking 'slavery' as the paradigm of atrocity defined coercion as *physical* violence. That sanitised debt-driven indenture and 'free' wage labour as voluntary contract, and redeemed empire as humanitarian. Imperialism, humanitarianism and capitalism are 'elective affinities'.
readings.context: A historical case study of [[kennedy-hr-problem]]'s claims: insulating the economy, condemnation as legitimation, the West and the Rest. With [[johnson-slavery]] on the costs of the 'inhuman' frame. Empire and the civilising mission connect to [[anghie-imperialism]], [[becker-lorca-mestizo]] and [[maine-kathiawar]]. Free contract as the market's form recalls [[roepke-1955]] and [[cohen-property-sovereignty]].

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Spring Break: The Activist Individual (recommended)
readings.summary:
Ch. 2 of *The Dark Sides of Virtue*: the activist individual.

**The mission.** March 1984. Kennedy (lawyer), Dr Richard Goldstein (doctor) and Patrick Breslin (writer) represent five US scientific and medical institutions. They become the first outsiders to speak privately with Uruguay's roughly 700 political prisoners. The story opens with Ana Rivera, 23, trembling, wearing all her clothes for fear of transfer.

**Telling vs doing.** Both analysis and activism respond to 'narrative demands'. They turn the confusion of moments like the one with Ana into stories (strategy, the evolution of law, democratisation), 'embroidering it into the fabric of numerous comforting stories'. The familiar plot is the knight errant who returns 'with tales aplenty'; his words take precedence over her suffering.

**Thinking ahead.** He was drawn by escape from grading midterms, excitement and the exotic. Doubts about standing ('what right did I have?') and fear of disorientation followed. The team memorised and shredded briefing documents so as to look innocuous yet potent.

**Crossing over (Punta Rieles women's prison).** Warden Kleber Papillon recites his script; the team nods. The delegation's 'hollow' institutional story ('our sponsors are interested in' specific prisoners; 'public health, not public policy') wins cooperation. The warden proudly says he learned prison management from the American military.

**Professional roles.** Activism is representational and sponsored. Scientific institutions fear losing neutrality. Harvard frames foreign advocacy as neutral 'rule of law'. Roles script the barbarian as 'rights abuser' and the victim as 'client'. They channel outrage into 'a rhetoric of health' and Ana's politics into a physical exam. Roles are stepping stones and walls. The team becomes friends by playing with roles (Richard/the Doctor). Analysis settles ambiguity only by treating a detail as dispositive.

**Direct examination.** The lawyer steers Ana toward the legally relevant facts; the doctor says let her narrate. Her account of torture breaks the 'cassette'. 'I have lost interest in the case'; he fixates on her string bracelets. The women's stories blend. Should he assess credibility? Refusing to judge it puts her 'on a pedestal of untouchable authenticity'; judging it reduces the experience. 'Trapped between the necessity and the danger.'

**Cross-examination (prison doctor).** He wants to cross-examine the doctor 'to the wall' with the UN code on health workers and torture. The more the doctor confirms abuse, the better the cross-examination feels. Richard offers professional solidarity and the doctor escapes. Goals conflict: blame, change behaviour, bear witness, reinforce norms. Doing good vs doing well. A memory of a Paris physician turning suffering into a demand to *declare* a 'right to health': 'not health, but a right to health; not engagement, but declaration'. Worrying about standing is a way to deny that the relationship is personal: 'our secret desire to take one more look at the wound'.

**Libertad (men's prison).** A harsher regime, with photographs of Tupamaro victims on the walls. Interviews happen on phones behind glass. Ramon (Ana's boyfriend) and Francisco tell of torture as 'temporarily defeated warriors': comrades who need no rescue. Victor, the apolitical veterinarian, pleads procedure and rekindles the urge to *act* ('The position').

**Transition: gender.** The drive back separates a sphere of violation (women, victims, the sacred) from a field of response (men, avengers, Montevideo). Ana was 'trespassed upon', Ramon 'punished'. Manipulating this gender distinction produced 'simultaneous engagement and distance'.

**Advocacy.** Night meetings with Uruguayan lawyers; one says the trials are 'the imitation of trials' and that representing prisoners means 'not to forget them'. He drops international law (no theory of standing) for humanitarian pleading. Before Colonel Ledesma of the Supreme Military Court there is the protocol of the red chairs and 'lawyer to lawyer' talk. Ledesma insists the court is independent while discussing pending files. Both men are 'polite, respectful, and cynical'.

**Aftermath.** Families ask why *these* prisoners. US embassy: 'we … send them up to Panama, and tell them about constitutions'. Guilt at leaving: the bureaucracy is 'the machinery of our mutual estrangement'. Human rights 'plays an important role in sustaining the very image of irrationality to which it purports to be merely responding'. 'Even if you don't get inside the prisons, you'll have struck a blow' — the mission needed torture only to be 'out there'. 'As human rights activists, we can touch the barbaric and return unscathed.' 'Our discourse is not our tool; we are its property.'

**Epilogue (1985).** All the students were released. Ledesma asked the writer for advice on New York publishers for his short stories.
arguments: Narrating and doing human rights both convert ambiguity into comforting stories.
Professional roles enable contact but produce estrangement and complicity.
Gendered images (female victim, male avenger) structure the activist's sense of progress.
The rights vocabulary lets advocates engage atrocity while keeping it 'out there'.
The activist is the discourse's property, not its master.
readings.tldr: A first-person account of a 1984 human rights mission (writer–doctor–lawyer) to Uruguay's political prisons. Professional roles both enable contact and estrange. Telling and doing human rights both turn ambiguity into comforting stories. Gendered images (female victim, male avengers) structure the mission. The human rights vocabulary lets the advocate 'touch the barbaric and return unscathed'. 'Our discourse is not our tool; we are its property.'
readings.context: The lived, first-person version of [[kennedy-hr-problem]] (representation, bad faith, false solidarity, the 'imaginary third eye'). Gender analysis connects to [[knop-feminism-sovereignty]] and [[charlesworth-chinkin-jus-cogens]]. The voyeuristic victim parallels [[johnson-slavery]]. US training of the warden is the background-norms point again. Compare the professional sensibility of [[koh-tlp]] (transnational norm entrepreneurs) and [[riles-aspiration-control]].

readings.author: Philippe Sands
readings.title: Greening International Law, Parts Two & Three (recommended)
readings.summary:
Introduction (Parts Two–Three) to *Greening International Law* (1994). Parts of the scan are heavily garbled.

**The state of the field.** Environmental issues moved from the margins to the centre (UN, GATT). There are so many negotiations that only rich states can keep coherent positions. Yet there is 'reason to doubt' real impact: weak implementation; law-making that is decentralised, duplicative, reactive and ad hoc.

**Principles of general application** (Dworkin's distinction: rules apply all-or-nothing, principles 'state a reason that argues in one direction'):
- **Sovereignty over natural resources vs the responsibility not to cause environmental damage**: Stockholm Principle 21 / Rio Principle 2, widely seen as customary law. Sovereignty is 'tempered' by protection in an interdependent world.
- **Preventive principle**: minimising damage as an objective in itself, even within a state's own territory, and early.
- **Good neighbourliness and cooperation** (UN Charter art. 74 extended): information, notification, consultation, EIA, emergency cooperation. Central in Hungary v. Slovakia over the Gabčíkovo dam (referred to the ICJ in 1993).
- **Sustainable development**: roots in the Pacific Fur Seal Arbitration (1893). Four elements: intergenerational preservation, 'sustainable/prudent/rational' use, equitable use, and integrating environment and development.
- **Precautionary principle** (Rio Principle 15): lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone measures. 'Potentially, the most radical' and the most controversial.
- **Polluter pays**: status doubtful outside the EC, OECD and UN/ECE.
- **Common but differentiated responsibility** (Climate Convention): a common duty plus differing contributions and capacities.

**Standards.** Agenda 21's priorities (atmosphere, land, forests, biodiversity, freshwater, oceans) and harmful products (biotech, toxic chemicals, agriculture, hazardous and radioactive wastes). Regulating sector by sector shifts harm between media, hence integrated pollution control. Regimes surveyed:
- *Flora and fauna*: CITES, biodiversity, the IWC whaling moratorium of 1982; a forests convention failed at UNCED.
- *Marine*: UNCLOS and the Regional Seas programme. Land-based sources cause more than 70% of marine pollution and have no global treaty.
- *Freshwater*: rivers and lakes.
- *Air*: LRTAP, ozone (Vienna/Montreal) and the UNFCCC.
- *Waste*: Basel (prior informed consent), Lomé IV and Bamako (bans).
- *Hazardous substances*: soft law.

**Techniques.** Beyond 'command and control': EIA, information, liability, economic instruments (trade, IP, finance), and enforcement and dispute settlement. Montreal set the first timetable to ban production outright; the Antarctic Protocol bans commercial activity. Even an EC broadcasting directive bars ads encouraging environmentally harmful behaviour.
arguments: Environmental law is built on the tension between sovereignty over resources and no transboundary harm.
General principles (prevention, precaution, polluter pays, CBDR) guide rather than dictate.
Regulation is sectoral, so harm shifts between media.
Newer techniques: EIA, information, liability, economic instruments.
Proliferating instruments, weak implementation.
readings.tldr: Introduction to the 1990s field of international environmental law. Built on two opposed principles, sovereignty over resources vs no transboundary harm (Stockholm Principle 21 / Rio Principle 2), plus prevention, cooperation, sustainable development, precaution, polluter pays, and common but differentiated responsibilities. Then sector-by-sector standards and newer techniques (EIA, information, liability, economic instruments). Impressive output, doubtful impact.
readings.context: Sovereignty limited by harm to others descends from [[corfu-1949]] (no use of territory to harm others) and [[island-of-palmas]] (sovereignty's duties). Gabčíkovo is [[gabcikovo]]. Principles vs rules recalls [[schachter-general-principles]] and [[schachter-twilight]] (soft law). [[kennedy-hr-problem]] holds up this standards-based environmental regime as a better model than rights. [[falk-environment]] explains why it underperforms; [[siddique-ecocide]] turns to criminal law.
