readings.author: Richard Falk
readings.title: Environmental Protection in an Era of Globalization (recommended)
readings.summary:
Yearbook of International Environmental Law (1995), excerpts.

**Hypothesis.** Economic globalisation and environmental protection pursue 'fundamentally inconsistent policy objectives'. They could be reconciled only by effective regulatory authority based on a political equilibrium between economistic and environmentalist constituencies. That equilibrium does not exist and is unlikely, which reflects 'a deepening … comprehensive crisis of public goods'.

**Why 'globalization'.** It is a buzzword, but needed to name forces beyond the state, the state system and international institutions. Unlike economists who note earlier eras of trade, Falk stresses regulatory imperatives beyond the capacity and will of states. The state is not bypassed but *deterritorialised*: it loses autonomy to global market pressures and risks conflict with disadvantaged parts of its own society. The old world-order worry was fragmented sovereignty and the free-rider problem in the commons. The new one has a different cause and similar effects: all governments are disciplined by global capital, and exclusion (North Korea, Cuba, Iraq) means misery. The market is 'the only game in town'.

**Neo-liberal convergence.** Labour, the Democrats, the Socialists, regrouped Communists and even Nordic welfare parties have become de facto converts. Fiscal crisis cuts every public good, including the environment. Environmental costs are incompatible with privatisation, growth, low taxes and a non-intrusive state. Uneven conditions mean some feel no responsibility and others feel unfairly burdened. Widening gaps between rich and poor generate job anxiety, so 'the environmental movement … has run out of steam'. Since Rio (1992) this has got worse. Reviving the welfare-state social contract may require 'an unprecedented global social contract'.

**No determinism.** Globalisation is levelling up many poorer societies in the short term. The affluent states that led on the environment are the ones now under strain, while rising states focus on development. One hopeful scenario: a growing middle class brings environmental consciousness.

**Conclusions.** (1) Consider environmental impacts in economic policy. (2) The main effect so far is weaker support for public spending on (especially global) environmental goals. (3) Change requires an alternative to neo-liberalism in national politics. (4) Anti-globalisation backlashes and regionalism may offer the best short-term prospects. It is globalisation *as shaped by neo-liberalism*, not globalisation as such; a different climate could produce global environmental governance to match the economic kind. Cites the NIEO declaration.
arguments: Neo-liberal globalisation structurally weakens environmental regulation.
The state is deterritorialised and disciplined by global capital.
Mainstream parties converge; public goods are starved.
Economic insecurity drains political support for environmentalism.
Not inevitable: it requires an ideological alternative or a global social contract.
readings.tldr: Globalisation shaped by neo-liberalism exerts a structural 'downward pull' on environmental protection. States lose autonomy to global capital; mainstream parties converge on neo-liberalism; fiscal austerity starves public goods; insecurity drains support for environmental priorities. Globalisation is not inherently anti-environment, but changing course needs a new ideological climate or a 'global social contract'.
readings.context: The political-economy explanation for the weak implementation [[sands-greening]] notes. It reverses [[roepke-1955]]'s hope that depoliticising the economy serves order, and challenges [[bello-wto]]'s confidence in trade disciplines. NIEO: [[bedjaoui-nieo]]. Compare [[kennedy-hr-problem]] on insulating the economy.

readings.author: Haroon Siddique
readings.title: Legal Experts Worldwide Draw up 'Historic' Definition of Ecocide (recommended)
readings.summary:
Guardian report (22 June 2021).
- **Definition**: 'unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts'.
- **Significance**: it would be the fifth ICC crime (alongside war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and aggression) and the first new international crime since Nuremberg. Sands: the others focus 'exclusively on the wellbeing of human beings'; this one introduces 'a new non-anthropocentric approach'. It is mostly about 'changing public consciousness' that we depend on the environment.
- **History**: Olof Palme at Stockholm (1972); dropped from the Rome Statute in 1998; Polly Higgins' decade-long campaign (d. 2019).
- **Support**: Vanuatu and the Maldives (2019 ASP), Macron, the Pope, some European states. The ICC was criticised for ignoring environmental crimes; in 2016 it said it would consider environmental destruction and land grabs within existing crimes.
- **Design choice**: no explicit mention of climate change, to make it harder for states and corporations to oppose. It aims at the 'most egregious acts', not the everyday activity 'so many of us … are involved in'. Examples: transboundary nuclear accidents, major oil spills, Amazon deforestation, killing the last two northern white rhinos.
- Stop Ecocide's Jojo Mehta: 'well pitched between what needs to be done … and what will be acceptable to states'.
arguments: Proposes ecocide as the fifth core international crime.
Non-anthropocentric: the environment itself as the protected interest.
Calibrated to egregious acts and to state acceptability (no climate clause).
Expressive aim: changing public consciousness.
readings.tldr: In June 2021 an expert panel (co-chaired by Philippe Sands and Dior Fall Sow) proposed adding 'ecocide' to the Rome Statute as the fifth ICC crime: 'unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and widespread or long-term damage to the environment'. It is billed as the first non-anthropocentric international crime. Climate change is deliberately left unmentioned, to keep states on board.
readings.context: Moves environmental law from the cooperative principles of [[sands-greening]] to individual criminal responsibility. It inherits the dilemmas of [[koskenniemi-impunity]], [[engle-grip]] and [[drumbl-smouldering]], and [[kennedy-hr-problem]]'s 'condemnation as legitimation'. Excluding everyday harm is the background vs exception point. Reappears in [[burgis-kasthala-gaza]].

readings.author: Burgis-Kasthala & Masetti Placci
readings.title: Lost for Words, yet Grasping for Neologisms: Gaza, Genocide and the Discursive Limits of International Law
readings.summary:
EJIL: Talk! post (Nov. 2024), with Matilde Masetti Placci. The excerpt omits p. 2 and the ending.

**Thesis.** 'Genocide' carries explosive expressive power. Speakers resist the normalisation of suffering through *genocide anachronisms* (broad conceptions overlooked in the 1948 definition) and *genocide neologisms* (recent efforts at analysis or norm creation). The 'cacophony of criminalisation' tries to undercut genocide's rigidities, especially intent and physical destruction. It builds on law rather than rejecting it, and reflects scholars' 'widespread need … to have their respective fields be seen as relevant'. 'Genocide and its related cides' often crowd out other paradigms such as crimes against humanity.

**Older terms.** *Sociocide* (Russell Tribunal 2013: 'the systematic destruction of the essence of a social group', invoked for its expressive power and set against self-determination). *Politicide* (Kimmerling 2003). *Economicide* and 'de-development' (Sara Roy). Much of this came from outside international law, out of fear that the law cannot capture Palestinian experience.

**New and reinvigorated cides.**
- *Medicide*: attacks on hospitals, personnel and vehicles; links to art. II(d) (births prevented) and beyond, to long-term reproduction and quality of life.
- *Scholasticide*: more than 600,000 students lost a year; about 11,000 university students and more than 500 teachers killed. Art. II(e) is silent on education's link to group identity. The Central Archives were bombed (*memoricide*).
- *Domicide/spaciocide/urbicide*: more than two-thirds of buildings destroyed; displacement of over 90%. Common space is the prerequisite of collective identity; 'safe zones' are targeted.
- *Ecocide*: from Agent Orange in Vietnam. Destruction of land and agriculture 'ungrounds' Indigenous people; Forensic Architecture finds changes to Gaza's geology. It disrupts anthropocentric victimhood: 'Genocide cannot encompass this type of harm.' The Rome Statute amendment was formally proposed in September 2024, and the ICC has jurisdiction over Palestine since 2014.

**Full circle: Nakba.** Grinberg (2009) disdained neologisms for 'The Thing without a Name' as vulnerable to caveats, and preferred Arabic terms. 'Nakba' entered English legal discourse via South Africa at the ICJ (Dec. 2023), as both a historical event and an ongoing process.
arguments: Genocide's legal limits (intent, physical destruction) drive proliferating neologisms.
Each 'cide' names a dimension of group destruction: health, education, space, environment, memory.
Neologisms aim at relevance and expressive power more than doctrine.
Genocide talk can crowd out other legal paradigms.
Nakba as an older, non-legal name for an ongoing process.
readings.tldr: Faced with Gaza, speakers of the law reach beyond 'genocide' to a proliferation of 'cides': sociocide, politicide, medicide, scholasticide, domicide/spaciocide/urbicide, ecocide, memoricide. These are attempts to escape genocide's narrow intent and physical-destruction requirements. They are not a rejection of law but a struggle to stay relevant. The circle closes on 'Nakba' as a word for an ongoing process.
readings.context: A coda on the expressive and discursive limits of law. It tests [[kennedy-hr-problem]]'s worry that naming atrocity can be a way of not responding, and the law/non-law boundary ([[schachter-twilight]]). Ecocide links to [[siddique-ecocide]]. The criminal-law turn is examined in [[engle-grip]], [[koskenniemi-impunity]] and [[drumbl-smouldering]]. Compare [[rychter-emoji]] on law's vocabulary under strain.

readings.author: Roland Barthes
readings.title: The Eiffel Tower
readings.cite: The Eiffel Tower and Other Mythologies, 3
readings.summary:
Essay (1964; trans. 1979) opening Topic 16 ('Institutions as Governance').

**Omnipresence.** Maupassant lunched in the Tower because it was the only place in Paris he didn't have to see it. It is 'as literal as a phenomenon of nature', a universal symbol of Paris, modernity, science, the 19th century, rocket, phallus, lightning rod. 'This pure — virtually empty — sign — is ineluctable, because it means everything.'

**Seeing and seen.** An object when we look at it, a lookout when we visit. 'A complete verb, both active and passive.' It transgresses 'the habitual divorce of seeing and being seen'. This gives it 'a prodigious propensity to meaning': a pure signifier into which people endlessly put meaning, never fixed.

**Uselessness.** To be a total monument it must 'escape reason'. Its uselessness was a scandal, so Eiffel listed scientific uses (aerodynamics, physiology of the climber, radio, meteorology). These seem 'quite ridiculous alongside the overwhelming myth'. 'Use never does anything but shelter meaning.' A 'Babel complex'. It is a 'zero degree of the monument': no rite, no cult, nothing inside, yet twice the visitors of the Louvre.

**The panorama.** Belvederes overlook nature; the Tower overlooks the city and makes it a kind of nature. With Hugo and Michelet it gives 'the world to read and not only to perceive': structure, 'concrete abstraction'. Every visitor 'makes structuralism without knowing it', deciphering landmarks and noticing what is missing (the Arc de Triomphe). The view becomes history: prehistoric sea, the Middle Ages (Notre-Dame, 'its Tower and its Cathedral'), the history of France, the new (UNESCO). Then social functions along an axis (pleasure, commerce, knowledge; residential vs blue-collar; the westward drift of wealth). Climbing it is an initiation, like the provincial's first conquest of Paris (Rastignac).

**Inside the object.** How can you visit a line? Technical paradoxes: oblique pillars, slanted elevators, a straight line made of countless segments. A familiar 'little world': commerce tames sacred sites, the restaurant brings comfort. 'Autarchy': one can dream, eat, observe, shop there, like on an ocean liner, 'cut off from the world and yet the owner of a world'.
arguments: Monuments work as empty signifiers that absorb meaning.
Utilitarian justifications shelter, rather than produce, an institution's meaning.
Seeing and being seen: the view from the top turns the world into readable structure.
Use, commerce and comfort domesticate the sacred.
Institutions as myth: their power is in the projections they attract.
readings.tldr: The Tower is an 'utterly useless', 'empty' monument, a 'pure signifier' that attracts meaning 'the way a lightning rod attracts thunderbolts'. Its utilitarian justifications (science, radio) only 'shelter meaning'. It both sees and is seen. Its panorama turns Paris into an intelligible structure ('concrete abstraction'), and visiting it is an initiation. Read as a lens: institutions as myths that work by being empty enough to hold every projection.
readings.context: A lens for the topic. Like the Tower, the League ([[corbett-league]]) and the UN ([[kennedy-sg]]) are justified by function but live as symbols onto which internationalists and sceptics project 'community' or 'sovereignty'. The panoramic, radial 'view from the centre' is what [[kennedy-sg]] rejects. Compare the symbolic work of form in [[riles-aspiration-control]] and [[kennedy-chart]]'s cycles of institutional faith.

readings.sub: League of Nations, the United Nations, and a History of Reform
readings.author: P.E. Corbett
readings.title: What is the League of Nations?
readings.summary:
British Year Book of International Law (1924), excerpts.

**Question.** The study must look at the League 'not merely as it is established … by the Treaties of Peace, but as a living organism'. The state is 'the person par excellence'. English and American writers say states are the only subjects; continental writers (Bluntschli, Fiore, Fauchille) admit others; most League writers affirm personality. It matters because handing common affairs to permanent organisations 'has reached a climax' in the League.

**Testing Oppenheim's list.**
- **Legation**: members keep officials at Geneva; the League sends agents and has privileges and immunities (art. 7). But the League cannot choose or refuse members' representatives, so its 'passive' side 'is not a right, but an absolute obligation'. It is 'only a power with some of the incidents' of legation. (It also cannot issue passports.)
- **War and peace**: claimed from arts. 10, 11 and 16, but the Council only 'recommends' to 'the several Governments concerned'. 'It is for each Member to determine whether it will … declare war.' This is where the League 'approaches most nearly the mere alliance'. There is no 'corporate *jus belli ac pacis*' (compare the German Confederation's Diet, which could decide war by a two-thirds majority).
- **Sovereignty**: in the Saar (Versailles art. 49) Germany renounces the *government*, not the sovereignty, to the League 'in the capacity of trustee'. The Governing Commission legislates, taxes and administers justice, but Germany keeps the *nuda proprietas* of sovereignty, the inhabitants keep German nationality, and a plebiscite follows in 1935. Mandates and Danzig get similar analysis.

**Conclusion.** These rights 'can only be exercised by sovereign States'. Proving them would prove too much: an entity hard to distinguish from the state, 'the invariably repudiated super-State'. But 'personality in international as in municipal law is simply distinct subjectivity to rights and duties'; the 'artificial' person is as 'real' as the human being. The objection that no sovereign above states can confer personality is just 'the argument that there is no international law dressed in another form'. It would equally disprove the state's own personality, which rests on recognition. Once international law exists, states 'can create what legal institutions they will'. 'The League of Nations, as the subject of rights and duties distinct from those of its Members and recognized by the vast majority of civilized countries, is a person of international law.'
arguments: Sovereign-like attributes claimed for the League are really limited, derivative powers.
War decisions remain with members: closer to an alliance than a corporate actor.
Saar: government without sovereignty (Germany keeps nuda proprietas).
Too much state-likeness would make it the feared super-State.
Personality = distinct rights and duties; states can create such persons.
readings.tldr: Is the League of Nations an international person? Corbett tests the sovereign-like attributes claimed for it (Oppenheim): legation, war and peace, sovereignty (Saar, mandates), intervention, protectorate (Danzig). Each turns out to be only a power with some incidents of the state's right. If the League really had them, it would be the 'invariably repudiated super-State'. Yet personality is simply distinct subjectivity to rights and duties, and states can create such persons. So the League *is* a person, of its own kind.
readings.context: The classic interwar framing of the institution question (person or agent of its members?) that [[kennedy-sg]] calls a red herring, using the same phrase *nuda proprietas*. Personality via recognition parallels statehood debates ([[montevideo]], [[damrosch-states]]). Functional powers anticipate [[jessup-functional]]. Trusteeship and mandates connect to [[anghie-imperialism]] and [[redslob-nationalities]]. The 'living organism' method echoes [[berman-modernism]].

readings.sub: Leadership as Governance – The Secretary General
readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Leader, Clerk or Policy Entrepreneur? The Secretary-General in a Complex World
readings.summary:
Chapter in Chesterman (ed.), *Secretary or General?* (2007).

**The false choice.** Leader vs clerk mirrors other design debates: legal personality vs agency, general vs functional immunity, withdrawal. New York worships the UN; Washington is 'US sovereignty all the time'. Both share a 'radial' picture, with power unrolling from a centre (the Secretariat, or the federal government holding the full *nuda proprietas* of sovereignty). In fact: 'Political power is an affair of overlapping networks, chaotic cross-influences, and plural perspectives.' Multilateralism is 'a game played on many boards at once' and 'a kind of religion'. The world is neither an anarchic void nor run by an international community; 'there is law and regulation at every turn'. Example: the US castigated Kofi Annan until he backed its reform push, and then the G-77 saw him as its lapdog.

**Diplomat.** The UN's convening role became obsolete early. It survived because decolonisation multiplied peripheral states. 'There simply is no such thing' as the international community: the phrase names elites who are the media's imagined audience. The UN is an institutional system 'like Microsoft or the Vatican or Japan or New York City'. Nor is there 'sovereignty': it is a claim some make about prerogatives. Even the President 'does not decide alone'; 'half of Washington wakes up every morning to ensure that the President does not succeed'. Expert consensus (Iraq WMD, credibility, dominoes) shapes war. Violence is now a tactic for everyone. The SG should be an 'impresario rather than star': knitting coalitions (NATO, the EU and the AU in Darfur); 'no surprises' for Council members; not isolating states (Iran, Myanmar), since isolation is itself a relationship. He should not pretend all sovereigns are equal; sovereign equality 'disconnects the United Nations from its real human clients', the dispossessed behind weak states. Instead he should build their participation (mobilise mayors, citizen juries), convene small ad hoc meetings, and exercise 'the power not to convene'.

**Policy-maker.** The UN moved from diplomacy to administration (peacekeeping, relief, Oil-for-Food), tracking the welfare state. But policy today is *regulatory*: 'complex constellations of diverse private and public ordering'. Law's fabric is 'lumpy' (universal-crime risk falls with distance from London or Brussels; California emissions standards; ISO 14000 via supply chains; Teubner's sectoral regimes). The UN still thinks in universal treaties and spending targets (the MDGs). Instead: abandon universal standards; build 'complex cocktails of regulation' that differ for cities and countryside, rich and poor. Labour norms are really the right mix of immigration, social security and tax law. Drugs for tropical diseases need a mix of IP, parallel-import, competition and insurance rules. Build capacity at the periphery: 'less universalism and less uniformity'.

**Ethics and the end of universalism.** The SG as 'secular Pope or Hollywood idol' (Annan as 'norm entrepreneur'). The dangers: enchanting institutions as substitutes for moral work, and provoking a counter-vision of the West and the rest. Principles 'travel in pairs'; even cartoons test the creed. The global consensus also legitimates suffering (property over medicines, sovereignty, self-defence). A diplomatic ethics is like an established church: 'not good for the government, not good for the church'. The 'site' of the universal is itself a local place. The task is to 'build bridges … among the world's quite different ethical worlds'.
arguments: Leader vs clerk, community vs sovereignty: a red herring rooted in a radial picture of power.
Neither 'international community' nor 'sovereignty' exists as such; power is dispersed.
The SG as impresario of shifting coalitions, not world's premier diplomat.
Regulation, not administration or universal treaties: 'cocktails' of diverse rules.
Ethical modesty: universalism provokes counter-visions and legitimates suffering.
readings.tldr: The century-old debate (strong 'leader' like Albert Thomas vs 'clerk' like Eric Drummond) is a red herring. Both internationalists (New York) and sovereigntists (Washington) imagine a radial world with a centre. In fact power is dispersed through networks and 'the capillaries of social and economic life'. There is no 'international community' and no 'sovereignty' as such. The SG should be a strong *policy entrepreneur*: an impresario of shifting coalitions, a catalyst for diverse regulatory experiments, and modest about universal ethics. 'Justice needs to be made anew in each time and in each place.'
readings.context: Applies the Kennedy critique ([[kennedy-hr-problem]]: 'community' as fantasy, justice made anew) to institutional design. Rejects the personality debate of [[corbett-league]] and the radial view Barthes's Tower embodies ([[barthes-eiffel]]). Hammarskjöld's 'cracks between the blocs' is [[schachter-hammarskjold]]. Networks and disaggregation echo [[slaughter-around-un]] and [[jessup-transnational]]. Regulation-as-governance leads to [[kingsbury-gal]] and Topic 17 ([[danielsen-local-rules]]). Isolation vs relationship complicates [[nyt-putin-ukraine]] and sanctions.

readings.author: Kingsbury, Krisch & Stewart
readings.title: The Emergence of Global Administrative Law
readings.tldr: Much global governance is really *administration*: rulemaking and decisions below treaty-making and outside dispute settlement, by formal IOs, networks, distributed national regulators, hybrid and private bodies. Its accountability deficit is generating a 'global administrative law' of transparency, participation, reasoned decisions, review and proportionality. Its normative basis is contested (regime integrity, rights, democracy), and it may entrench Northern power.
readings.summary:
Law & Contemporary Problems (2005), excerpts. Founding statement of the NYU 'GAL' project.

**Diagnosis.** A vast increase in transgovernmental regulation (security, aid conditions, environment, banking, telecoms, trade, IP, labour, refugees) has shifted decisions to the global level. They are often implemented by bodies not controlled by national governments. Result: an *accountability deficit*. Two responses: extend domestic administrative law to global decisions, and build new global mechanisms.

**Definition.** GAL comprises 'the mechanisms, principles, practices, and supporting social understandings that promote or otherwise affect the accountability of global administrative bodies'. It means transparency, participation, reasoned decision, legality and effective review. Administrative action = rulemaking, adjudications and decisions that are 'neither treaty-making nor simple dispute settlements'.

**The global administrative space: five types.**
1. *Formal IOs*: Security Council sanctions committees acting on individuals; UNHCR status determinations and camps.
2. *Transnational networks*: e.g. the Basle Committee (central bankers; non-binding but effective).
3. *Distributed administration*: national regulators acting in a global regime (e.g. extraterritorial regulation).
4. *Hybrid public-private*: Codex Alimentarius (quasi-binding via the SPS Agreement), ICANN.
5. *Private bodies*: ISO (over 13,000 standards), fair-trade and timber certification, SWIFT, the Fair Labor Association. In the global sphere they 'often have greater power'.
Its subjects are not only states but individuals, firms and NGOs. Hence a distinct global administrative space: international lawyers can no longer say accountability runs through states to voters; domestic lawyers can no longer say domestic review suffices.

**Ambivalence.** Administrative framing may stabilise and legitimate current power and 'Northern and Western concepts'. But it also creates 'a platform for critique': small developing countries are *already* 'administered' by the WTO, IMF, World Bank and Security Council. The focus is procedure, not substance.

**Mechanisms and doctrines.** Domestic courts checking IOs. Global disciplines on domestic regulators (WTO/GATS procedures, independent telecoms regulators, investment arbitration under ICSID and NAFTA, 'a very powerful tool' for investors). *Participation* (Shrimp-Turtle: the US had to give exporting states a hearing; NGOs in Codex). *Reasons* (the anti-doping regime). *Review* (the World Bank Inspection Panel, the Court of Arbitration for Sport). *Proportionality*, means-ends fit and least-restrictive means (ECHR; GATT).

**Normative bases** (English School: pluralism, solidarism, cosmopolitanism):
- (a) *intra-regime accountability* (least demanding; fits pluralism);
- (b) *protecting rights* of individuals or of states (contested in a pluralist order);
- (c) *democracy* (most demanding; no convincing global democratic theory; 'deliberative technocracy' is inadequate once distributive choices loom).
A pragmatic route: incremental participation and review.

**Who shapes it?** Its models are European and American. It may need an 'overlapping consensus'. Against the radical critique that global institutions are 'imperial': reform vs revolution, 'both sides … probably right'. Most proposals increase accountability toward Northern populations and markets; real reform may require empowering the South.
arguments: Global governance is largely administration by diverse public, hybrid and private bodies.
An accountability deficit drives emerging GAL norms: transparency, participation, reasons, review.
Five types of global administration; individuals and firms as subjects.
Normative foundations contested: regime integrity, rights, democracy.
GAL may legitimate Northern dominance unless it empowers the South.
readings.context: Turns [[kennedy-sg]]'s 'age of regulation' into a legal programme. It builds on the network vision of [[slaughter-around-un]] and [[jessup-transnational]], and on [[schachter-twilight]] (non-binding but effective norms). Shrimp-Turtle and the WTO connect to [[bello-wto]]; investment arbitration to Topic 14. Private standard-setters lead to Topic 17 ([[danielsen-local-rules]], [[iglp-gvc]]). [[miller-parity]] shows administration and expertise in practice in Palestine. The 'imperial institutions' critique links to [[anghie-imperialism]] and [[chimni-2017]].

readings.author: Zinaida Miller
readings.title: Perils of Parity: Palestine's Permanent Transition
readings.summary:
Cornell International Law Journal (2014), excerpts.

**Thesis.** In 1993 came the 'triumph of hope over history'; by 2014 the crisis was 'more about preserving the process than finding a path to peace'. The Oslo regime matters 'as much for the system it produced as for the solution it failed to provide'. International ideas, donor aid and expertise now dominate the routine management of the territories. International involvement turned occupation 'into an indefinite "transition" in which two organized entities face one another in negotiations as notional equals', while public life shifts 'from political resistance to institution-building, economic development, and security'.

**Background: occupation (1967–93).** Occupation balances the occupier's security against the welfare of the occupied, and assumes temporariness. Israel initially denied that the Hague and Geneva rules applied, then applied the 'humanitarian' provisions de facto; the Supreme Court applied the Hague Regulations. Military orders governed daily life. Prolonged occupation produced uneven integration, which later 'neutral' agreements built on. Under Oslo (1993–2013) occupation law still applied, but zones (most land under Israeli control) and a Palestinian Authority limited in power and corrupted over time turned a bilateral relationship 'into a tripartite system of governance'.

**International governance.** After the Cold War, peace became a field of expertise: statebuilding, development, human rights, humanitarianism, 'post-conflict' intervention. Aid phases: building peace (1993–2000), managing crisis (2000–06), confronting statehood (2006–13). Costs: subsidy, infrastructure, mitigation.

**Parity.** Bilateral talks with an 'impartial' mediator; people-to-people dialogues of 'equally valid narratives'. Mutual recognition was asymmetrical: the PLO recognised Israel's 'right … to exist in peace and security'; Israel recognised the PLO only as a representative, 'in light of the PLO commitments'. Abbas (2011): 'a test of our worthiness, entitlement and eligibility'. Defining 'peace' as the shared goal made sovereignty 'a bargaining chip'. 'All the trappings of statehood' while destitute. The word 'occupation' fades. Resistance shifts from ending occupation to statehood, away from liberation. The World Bank judges the PA 'as a state' while statehood is denied.

**Economism.** Aid aimed to make peace more attractive than violence ('peace dividend'). Netanyahu's 'economic peace' and Fayyad's statebuilding-as-resistance shared one vocabulary. Development moved from a link between economics and politics to a wedge between them ('development regardless of occupation'), serving the status quo.

**Transition.** Rhetorical transience covers practical permanence, mirroring occupation's own contradiction. The 1995 Paris Protocol customs union was presented as neutral status quo. The progress narrative has an under-specified endpoint (two states…) plus escalating conditions mostly on Palestinians (elections, recognition, Charter revision, leadership change). UNSCO reports: aid → PA → only hope for peace. Human rights and transitional justice were kept off the table. Autesserre: the 'post-conflict' label makes some policies natural and others illegitimate. Aid punishes Hamas's election and the UN bid. 'A transitional regime, by its nature, resists criticism.'

**Conclusion.** Ideas and institutions, and local and international actors, shape each other iteratively. Resistance uses the regime's vocabulary (Bennett's Area C annexation; the UN-membership bid). Abbas: 'send a junior officer … and we'll give him the keys'. Above all, Oslo converted occupation 'into a series of discrete topics to be managed and negotiated rather than adjudicated'; 'issues once argued as law became … questions of policy'. The regime 'concealed inequality behind parity, masked political stakes with economic technocracy, and hidden permanence under transition'.
arguments: Oslo's lasting product is a regime of international aid and expertise, not peace.
Parity: formal equality of negotiating parties masks structural asymmetry.
Economism: development as peacebuilding depoliticises the occupation.
Permanent transition: a progress narrative with escalating conditions on the weaker party.
Law displaced by policy: occupation managed rather than adjudicated.
readings.tldr: The Oslo Accords failed to end the conflict but produced a durable 'regime' of international money and expertise. It reframed occupation as a 'permanent transition' with three features. *Parity*: two notionally equal negotiating parties, masking asymmetry. *Economism*: development as peacebuilding, crowding out distribution and resistance. *Transition*: a progress narrative with an elusive endpoint and conditions imposed mostly on Palestinians. Questions once argued as law became questions of policy.
readings.context: Institutions and expertise as governance on the ground: the critical counterpart to [[kingsbury-gal]]. Statehood without sovereignty and conditional recognition connect to [[montevideo]], [[damrosch-states]] and [[berman-jerusalem]]. Economism parallels [[kennedy-hr-problem]] (form over substance, insulating politics) and [[nesiah-slavery-afterlives]] (protection masking structure). Gaza's later fate: [[burgis-kasthala-gaza]]. Transition and expertise anticipate [[oconnell-ihl]] and Topic 20's law of war.

readings.author: Dan Danielsen
readings.title: Corporate Power and Global Order
readings.tldr: Corporations are not the 'private' other of the regulating state but legal institutions that *govern*. They pressure regulators, acquiesce in or interpret rules (setting the de facto rule), ignore rules they won't be made to follow, and write their own standards. So *corporate law* is a lever of global governance: home-state rules on board representation, fiduciary duty and takeovers shape wages, safety and the environment abroad.
readings.summary:
Chapter in Orford (ed.), *International Law and its Others* (2006), excerpts.

**Claim.** From the East India Companies to modern MNEs, international law has treated corporations as objects of regulation, influences on it, or forces that escape it, never as producers of regulation. Danielsen proposes seeing them as 'legal institutions performing public regulatory functions with public welfare effects not unlike nation-states'.

**How corporations govern.** (1) *Pressure*: lobbying, studies, campaigns, threats to invest or disinvest; the public body can become the 'agent of' corporate power. (2) *Acquiescence*: accepting a contested rule legitimates it and emboldens the regulator. (3) *Interpretation*: where no authority settles applicability, corporate behaviour 'defines de facto the margins and meanings of legal rules'. (4) *Non-compliance* when enforcement is unlikely; compliance is 'overwhelmingly voluntarily controlled'. (5) *Own rules*: contracts, arbitration, standards on wages and safety, voluntary internationalisation (ISO 9000).

**Corporate governance as global governance.** Corporate law works like other 'constitutional' regimes (EU law, trade).
- *Board representation*: German co-determination (Roe) may shape wage and safety decisions wherever German firms operate. It may also protect home workers at foreign workers' expense.
- *Minority partners*: a local 40% partner in a subsidiary has no voice or standing at the parent, where the decisions are made. Home or host rules could change that.
- *Fiduciary duty*: hypothetical World Corp (incorporated in Zutopia) builds a plant in Bandu, which has no wastewater rules; Zutopia's environmental law doesn't reach abroad. Under the business judgment rule directors face no personal liability for dumping toxic wastewater, so the corporate decision becomes Bandu's de facto rule. Strict or negligence liability at home would change the calculus.
- *Hostile takeovers*: neo-liberal 'best practice' bans defences, but building national firms may need them (capturing gains from trade). The trade-offs are real, but these are policy choices, not neutral necessities.

**Why so little resistance?** The neo-liberal picture of one vast, nearly perfect global market. In fact it is multiple, overlapping regimes with more market failures, and corporations regulate to entrench advantage like any regulator.

**Lessons.** Corporations treat regulatory complexity as opportunity (arbitrage); scholars should too. Map corporate decisions 'with the same attention … that international lawyers … have applied to state activity'. Changing fiduciary rules in a few home jurisdictions might do more than lobbying for standards in every developing country.
arguments: Corporations govern: through pressure, acquiescence, interpretation, non-compliance and private rule-making.
Private/public is the wrong frame; corporations perform public regulatory functions.
Home-state corporate law (boards, fiduciary duties, takeovers) has global welfare effects.
The global economy is fragmented, not a perfect market; corporations entrench advantage.
Corporate governance rules are a neglected site for progressive intervention.
readings.context: Extends [[cohen-property-sovereignty]] (private power as sovereignty) and challenges [[roepke-1955]]'s depoliticised market. The legal personality question for IOs ([[corbett-league]]) is not asked of corporations. Extraterritoriality and the reach of home law: [[american-banana]], [[restatement-402-404]], [[bank-nova-scotia]]. Private standard-setters as administrators: [[kingsbury-gal]]. Developed further in [[danielsen-local-rules]] and [[iglp-gvc]].

readings.author: Dan Danielsen
readings.title: Local Rules and a Global Economy: An Economic Policy Perspective
readings.summary:
Transnational Legal Theory (2010), Part 1 (pp. 49–68).

**Local rules, global effects.** The 2008 crisis showed how US state and federal rules on mortgage lending, credit, derivatives and bankruptcy shaped the world. California emissions rules move supply chains and R&D; Chinese wage and labour standards set wages elsewhere; Chinese coal plants deposit mercury in the US West. 'Our increasingly global economy is governed principally by local rules created by local institutions designed to serve primarily … local policy interests.' No invisible hand turns this into global welfare.

**More global rules?** Not obviously. Universal rules reflect 'a negotiated balance of sovereign interests', especially of the powerful (Posner, Anghie, Chang; BIT preambles vs coercive reality). No global institution can do the welfare-state work of trading off and legitimating policy, and none is coming. Coordination among states frames talks around sovereign rights.

**The proposal.** A 'global economic policy perspective': an orienting posture like corporate counsel serving 'the corporation as a whole' or a judge's 'best interests of the child'. Not objectivity, but a basis for contestation.

**Coase's four uses.** (1) The economy is structured by myriad *background* local rules, not just international or extraterritorial ones. (2) Look at effects regardless of jurisdiction or intent: rules 'travel'. (3) Without transaction costs affected foreign constituencies would bargain over rules that affect them, so recognise them. (4) With transaction costs they can't, so *power asymmetries* matter.

**Limits of current frameworks.** *Public international law* (Restatement §§402–403) asks about jurisdictional basis and reasonableness between sovereigns. It misses de facto effects and needs express intent for responsibility. *Trade law* (Jackson's 'liberal trade') polices 'protectionism' and treats reduced local 'distortions' as welfare-enhancing. It leaves background rules as 'normal' and uses 'achievable inter-sovereign bargains as a proxy for global welfare'. Sometimes stricter *local* rules (e.g. G-20 bank regulation) beat a negotiated global rule.

**Power.** Sovereignty has an emancipatory history (decolonisation, citizenship), and national politics was 'better politics than anything that came before'. But formal sovereign equality (Montevideo art. 4) hides that US, Chinese or Japanese assertions matter far more than those of Cambodia or Uruguay. Anti-dumping remedies are formally open to all, but only the big use them well. The WTO 'multilateralises bilateral bargains' in favour of the large. Result: entrenching the divide between haves and have-nots. A new 'global vernacular' delinked from sovereignty is needed.
arguments: Local rules, not international ones, mainly govern the global economy.
Jurisdiction doctrine and trade law ask sovereignty questions, not global-welfare questions.
Inter-sovereign bargains are a poor proxy for global welfare.
Formal sovereign equality masks real asymmetries of regulatory power.
Coase as a critical tool to centre power and global welfare.
readings.tldr: The global economy is governed mainly by *local* rules: US mortgage and derivatives rules (2008), California emissions standards, Chinese wages and coal plants. International law asks only whether extraterritorial jurisdiction is lawful and 'reasonable'; trade law asks only whether a rule is 'protectionist'. Both use sovereign bargains as a proxy for global welfare and assume formal equality. A Coasean 'global economic policy perspective' would assess local rules by their global effects and expose power asymmetries.
readings.context: Critiques the jurisdiction framework of Topic 7 ([[restatement-402-404]], [[damrosch-jurisdiction]], [[berman-globalization-jurisdiction]]) and the trade frame of [[bello-wto]]. Formal equality vs real power echoes [[montevideo]], [[kennedy-sg]] and [[miller-parity]]. Background rules recall [[kennedy-hr-problem]] and [[cohen-property-sovereignty]]. Builds on [[danielsen-corporate]]; becomes the GVC agenda in [[iglp-gvc]].

readings.author: Adam Satariano
readings.title: The World's Tech Ambassador to the Tech Industry
readings.summary:
New York Times (3 Sept. 2019).
- Klynge (veteran of Afghanistan and Kosovo) calls this his toughest post. 'These companies have moved from being companies with commercial interests to actually becoming de facto foreign policy actors.' Denmark (5.8m people) is smaller than the Bay Area and under 0.3% of Facebook's users.
- Concerns: disinformation, privacy, cybersecurity, low taxes outside the US. Aim (FM Kofod): 'democratic governments set the boundaries for the tech industry and not the other way around'.
- Small-state diplomacy: Maldives' underwater cabinet; Sweden's Second Life embassy.
- Humbling: nine months to get a senior meeting, which ended in a T-shirt-and-cap goody bag. Microsoft's Brad Smith calls him well informed; Facebook says dialogue is now constructive.
- Leverage comes through the EU (privacy, competition, content; Vestager's fines).
- Criticised for putting corporations on a par with sovereigns; France, Australia, Britain and Germany have digital posts, mostly for trade. 'We aren't in the 1900s anymore.'
- Method: treat companies 'as if they were countries'; build networks with lower-level staff, ex-employees and civil society; send 'intelligence cables' home. A success: getting a terrorist murder video taken down.
arguments: Tech platforms act as foreign-policy actors with state-like power.
Diplomacy adapted to corporations: an embassy to Silicon Valley.
Small states lack leverage except through blocs (the EU).
Recognition and access: firms decide whom to receive.
readings.tldr: In 2017 Denmark appointed the world's first ambassador to the tech industry (Casper Klynge, based in Palo Alto), treating Facebook, Google and Apple as 'de facto foreign policy actors' and superpowers. Two years on: no meeting with Zuckerberg, Pichai or Cook. One executive ranted about EU regulation and handed him a goody bag. Small states struggle to be heard by firms bigger than they are.
readings.context: A concrete case of [[danielsen-corporate]] (corporations as governors) and [[kennedy-sg]] (power in networks, not sovereigns). Inverts recognition and legation ([[corbett-league]], [[montevideo]]): a state seeking audience with a company. Asymmetry among states: [[danielsen-local-rules]]. Pairs with [[nyt-musk]].

readings.author: IGLP Law and Global Production Working Group
readings.title: The Role of Law in Global Value Chains: A Research Manifesto
readings.tldr: Global value chains are usually explained by economics, with law as an external factor. The manifesto argues law (hard, soft and private ordering) is 'at the heart of the GVC phenomenon': it generates, captures and distributes value and coordinates production. Three research themes: legal geography, law-value-power, and law and chain 'governance'. Law shapes outcomes both when it acts and when it is absent.
readings.summary:
London Review of International Law (2016), IGLP Law and Global Production Working Group (Baars, Bair, Danielsen, Santos, White and others), excerpts.

**Premise.** GVCs arise not just from shareholder-value ideology, trade liberalisation or logistics, but as firms 'engage dynamically with multiple, overlapping and often conflicting' legal regimes, soft law and private ordering (together: 'law'). Almost every field is relevant: company, contract, employment, tax, trade, investment, human rights, environment, CSR codes, certification. A contract term may matter as much as a public regulation. Rather than asking how firms use law to 'upgrade', ask how upgrading possibilities are 'already structured in and through law'.

**1. Legal geography.** The MNC's 'make vs buy' choice already means corporate law vs contract law. Making abroad means comparing host laws and enforcement, trade, investment and IP rules. Buying means commercial law, standards and arbitration. Networks by contract rather than ownership may be about avoiding tort liability as much as productivity. Siting depends on enforcement likelihood and on unions, NGOs and lawyers. Extractives projects: Campling and Havice on tuna; Ovadia on local-content rules and the 'petro-developmental state'; White on Ghana's petroleum revenue laws and whether rents are distributed locally, nationally or supranationally.

**2. Law, value and power.** Open the 'black box' of value-added. Law creates barriers to entry and rents; entitlements shape bargaining power. Tax structuring shows that the location of value is 'as much a function of legal rules as production processes'. TRIPS let pharma keep global prices higher than under divergent national patent regimes (India, Brazil, Egypt). Labour law: export processing zones limit workers' activities and bar unions, keeping their 'value added' low; the rights to organise and strike affect both value and its capture; buyers' pricing affects labour standards upstream. Finance and financialisation. Family law, gender norms, welfare regimes and ethnic hierarchies also structure value. Non-regulation, non-enforcement, or a duty not to regulate (BITs vs local content) shapes outcomes: 'Law shapes power and value both when it seems to be acting and when it appears to be absent.'

**3. Governance** (coordination of chains) is the third theme. Bargaining power is 'as much a function of legal and policy choices as of "market forces"', so different choices could yield more equitable distributions.
arguments: Law is constitutive of GVCs, not an exogenous factor.
Legal geography: firms arbitrage regimes and enforcement in organising production.
Value and its distribution are legal artefacts (tax, IP, labour, finance).
Absence of law and non-enforcement also structure chains.
Different legal choices could redistribute power and rents.
readings.context: The research programme growing out of [[danielsen-corporate]] and [[danielsen-local-rules]]. Its legal-realist core comes from [[cohen-property-sovereignty]] (entitlements as power). It contrasts with [[roepke-1955]] and [[bello-wto]] on markets as natural. Private standards connect to [[kingsbury-gal]]; extraction and development to [[bedjaoui-nieo]] and [[chimni-2017]].

readings.author: The New York Times
readings.title: Elon Musk's Unmatched Power in the Stars
readings.summary:
New York Times (28 July 2023).
- **Scale**: more than 4,500 Starlink satellites, over 50% of active satellites, with plans for 42,000. Reusable rockets give SpaceX an 'express train' to orbit. Available in 50+ countries; 1.5m+ subscribers. Astronomers worry about the night sky and collisions. The company knows each terminal's location.
- **Ukraine**: after Russia's cyberattack on Viasat (Feb. 2022), Fedorov tweeted at Musk and service came within hours. More than 42,000 terminals; target-to-strike time cut from about 20 minutes to about 1. 'Starlink is indeed the blood of our entire communication infrastructure.' But Musk geofenced service (troops advancing into Kherson lost it), refused access near Crimea for a maritime drone attack, floated a peace plan with Russian annexation, and asked the Pentagon to pay (~$400m/year). About 1,300 terminals were cut off over unpaid fees. The Pentagon later bought terminals over which it controls geofencing. 'It has … been a long time since we've seen a company and an individual … go pretty openly against U.S. foreign policy in the middle of a war.'
- **Hedging**: Zaluzhnyi asked Milley for an assessment of Musk. At least nine countries raised concerns privately. Taiwan avoids Starlink because of Musk's China business (Tesla Shanghai) and signed with OneWeb. The EU funds a €2.4bn 'sovereign' constellation ('The E.U. cannot afford to be reliant on others'). SpaceX offers Starshield for governments.
- **Sovereignty clashes**: Iran says activating Starlink for protesters violated its sovereignty. China complains at the UN that SpaceX crowds orbit and sought assurance it won't be switched on there. Turkey refused it after the earthquake.
- 'This is not just one company, but one person … You are completely beholden to his whims.'
arguments: Critical infrastructure in private, personal hands with little oversight.
A private actor makes battlefield and foreign-policy decisions.
States hedge by building 'sovereign' alternatives.
Sovereignty claims (Iran, China, Turkey) against borderless private service.
readings.tldr: Elon Musk controls more than half of all active satellites through Starlink, which has become 'the blood' of Ukraine's military communications. With little regulation, one person can switch service on or off (geofencing near Crimea, refusing a drone strike, floating a pro-Russian 'peace plan'). Governments from Taiwan to the EU are hedging; Iran calls it a violation of sovereignty. Private infrastructure as geopolitical power.
readings.context: The extreme case of [[danielsen-corporate]]: a corporation (indeed a person) governing. With [[satariano-tech]]. War no longer a sovereign monopoly, as [[kennedy-sg]] argues; leads to Topic 20 ([[kristian-ukraine]], [[haines-weapons]]). Territorial sovereignty vs borderless technology: [[sassen-territory]], [[berman-globalization-jurisdiction]]. Ukraine context: [[nyt-putin-ukraine]].

readings.author: International Law Commission
readings.title: Fragmentation as a Phenomenon
readings.tldr: International law is splitting into specialised 'boxes' (trade, human rights, environment, investment, the law of the sea), each with its own principles, expertise and 'ethos'. MOX Plant: the same facts went before three fora. The ILC Study Group (Koskenniemi) treats this as both a danger and an expansion. Its answer is not hierarchy but a lawyer's 'toolbox' from the Vienna Convention: relationships of special/general, prior/later, hierarchy, and the 'normative environment' (systemic integration). 'Fragmentation and coherence … lie in the eye of the beholder.'
readings.summary:
ILC Study Group report, finalised by Martti Koskenniemi (2006), Ch. I paras. 5–20.

**Background.** Jenks (1953): with no general legislature, law-making treaties form separate 'historical, functional and regional groups', like separate municipal systems, so a conflict-of-laws analogy is needed. Today there are more than 50,000 treaties, plus regulatory regimes without a public-law orientation. Sociologists call this 'functional differentiation'. The paradox of globalisation: uniformisation *and* fragmentation. Specialist systems ('trade law', 'human rights law', 'environmental law', 'law of the sea', 'European law', 'investment law', 'refugee law') develop 'with relative ignorance' of their neighbours and of general law. Some see erosion and forum-shopping; others a technical problem.

**MOX Plant.** The Sellafield nuclear facility went to a UNCLOS Annex VII tribunal, an OSPAR tribunal and the European Court of Justice. Is it about the law of the sea, North Sea pollution, or EC relations? ITLOS: even identical rights in other treaties 'have a separate existence'; context, object and purpose, practice and *travaux* may make the same rule mean different things. What then of legal certainty and equality?

**Scope.** The Commission leaves institutional questions to the institutions themselves and focuses on substance: the 'splitting up of the law into highly specialized "boxes"'. The title (difficulties 'arising from the diversification and expansion') signals that the problems are neither new nor unmanageable. Each regime 'comes with its own principles, its own form of expertise and its own "ethos"'. Deviations are not 'mistakes' but reflect 'differing pursuits and preferences' in a pluralist society. Insisting on formal unity would be 'simultaneously utopian and authoritarian'.

**Approach.** Provide a conceptual framework from the professional's point of view: the 1969 VCLT, since all regimes claim force from the law of treaties. Functional fragmentation is 'not too different' from fragmentation into national legal systems. Four relationships: special/general (ch. II), prior/later (III), hierarchy (IV: only jus cogens invalidates; priority is usually 'relative'), and the 'normative environment' (V). This is not a set of ready-made solutions but 'a toolbox' for reasoned decision. 'Novelty presents itself as "fragmentation" of the old world'; reasoning makes the unfamiliar familiar.
arguments: Functional differentiation produces specialised regimes with their own ethos.
MOX Plant: one dispute, three fora, potentially different readings of the same rules.
Deviation reflects pluralist preferences; formal unity would be utopian and authoritarian.
Response: VCLT-based techniques (lex specialis, lex posterior, hierarchy, systemic integration).
Fragmentation and coherence are in the eye of the beholder.
readings.context: The doctrinal half of the Topic 3 report excerpted at [[ilc-fragmentation-jus-cogens]]. [[fischer-lescano-teubner]] calls this legal reductionism; [[lang-regimes]] asks how regimes' biases are made; [[koskenniemi-laws-rule-us]] widens the lens to the legal infrastructure of capitalism. Earlier fragmentation: [[jessup-functional]] and [[jessup-transnational]]. Regime proliferation is the world of [[kennedy-sg]] and [[kingsbury-gal]].

readings.author: Fischer-Lescano & Teubner
readings.title: Regime-Collisions: The Vain Search for Legal Unity in the Fragmentation of Global Law
readings.tldr: Luhmann predicted (1971) that global law would fragment along social sectors, not territories. Fragmentation is neither a legal problem of missing hierarchy nor merely 'policy conflicts' between actors. It reflects 'contradictions between society-wide institutionalized rationalities' (economy, science, health, technology), each of which has its own global law, including private regimes (lex mercatoria, lex digitalis) and 'auto-constitutional' regimes. Unity is a chimera ('lasciate ogni speranza'). At best a heterarchical 'weak normative compatibility' through networking and inter-regime conflicts law.
readings.summary:
Michigan Journal of International Law (2004), pp. 999–1018 in the packet.

**Two reductionisms.** About 125 international bodies now give final legal decisions. *Legal reductionism* sees missing doctrinal and judicial hierarchy and proposes hierarchy: ICJ appeals or advisory opinions (Schwebel, Guillaume), ILC 'no-hazard' certificates for new regimes (Hafner). *Political reductionism* (Koskenniemi and Leino) sees 'policy conflicts' between collective actors and proposes explicit politicisation. Correct but 'not deep enough'. (They chide Koskenniemi for softening the ILC title.)

**Thesis.** Legal fragmentation is 'an ephemeral reflection of a more fundamental, multi-dimensional fragmentation of global society'. Normative unity is 'doomed from the outset'. Fragmentation cannot be combated; at best weak compatibility via a network logic of 'loose coupling'.

**Social theory.**
- *A. Polycentric globalisation*: not just the economy. Autonomous global systems (science, culture, technology, health, the military, transport, sport…) each intensify their own rationality 'without regard' to others or the environment (Marx, Polanyi, Weber's polytheism, Luhmann). Problems such as finance, patents and cloning can't be solved by politics alone. 'The sin of differentiation can never be undone. Paradise is lost.'
- *B. Global law as a unitary system*, but unified by process ('inter-legality'), not by structure or consistency.
- *C. Sectoral differentiation* overlays territorial differentiation: regimes define their reach by issue, not territory.
- *D. Private regimes*: 'global law without the state'. Lex mercatoria, lex digitalis, the Apparel Industry Partnership, TRUSTe, ICANN. 'Self-juridification' of social fragments, not Krasner-style regimes.
- *E. Centre and periphery* replace hierarchy: courts at the centre; contracts, associations, standards and NGO consensus at the periphery. Self-contained regimes (Koskenniemi's definition) reproduce social conflicts: lex mercatoria vs WHO norms; lex constructionis vs environmental law; WTO vs human rights and environment; use of force vs human rights. Courts are coupled to their regimes, so the centre itself fragments ('polycontexturalization').
- *F. Auto-constitutional regimes*: Walker's seven criteria of constitutionalism applied to sectors (economy, science, sport). Regimes make their own secondary rules.

**Selective networking.** 'Lasciate ogni speranza': no apex or centre. Heterarchy: strengthen existing networks between regimes, and between regimes and their social sectors. Three principles: (1) normative compatibility instead of hierarchical unity; (2) law-making through mutual irritation, observation and reflexivity; (3) decentralised conflicts-of-laws methods. 'Final binding decision is replaced by a sequence of decisions' among network nodes. (The packet stops before the four examples: copyright, medicines, lex constructionis, *desaparición*.)
arguments: Legal fragmentation reflects collisions of social rationalities, not missing hierarchy or mere politics.
Global law is differentiated sectorally, including private and auto-constitutional regimes.
Courts are coupled to their regimes: no unifying centre.
Unity is unattainable; aim for weak compatibility via networking.
Inter-regime conflicts law on a private international law analogy.
readings.context: Responds to [[ilc-fragmentation-phenomenon]] (and its author) and to [[ilc-fragmentation-jus-cogens]]. Private regimes connect to [[danielsen-corporate]], [[kingsbury-gal]] and [[iglp-gvc]]. 'Society without an apex' echoes [[kennedy-sg]]; networks recall [[slaughter-around-un]]. [[lang-regimes]] questions treating regimes as given 'billiard balls'. Cites [[berman-globalization-jurisdiction]] (legal pluralism).

readings.author: Andrew T.F. Lang
readings.title: Legal Regimes and Professional Knowledges: The Internal Politics of Regime Definition
readings.tldr: Talk of 'regime interaction' risks reifying regimes as billiard balls with given biases. The trade regime is not free-market by mandate: what counts as a 'trade barrier' is indeterminate, so liberalisation first *constructs* some measures as distortions and backgrounds others. Its 'principles of vision' shifted from border barriers (embedded liberalism) to behind-the-border regulation after the 1970s, built by expert knowledge (e.g. the GATS Telecoms Reference Paper). Contestation must destabilise those visions, and expertise can be used to contest as well as entrench.
readings.summary:
Chapter in Young (ed.), *Regime Interaction in International Law* (2012), pp. 113–135 (some pages missing).

**Argument.** 'Coordination' and 'coherence' between regimes always mean hierarchising competing normative projects. But we must also study the *internal politics of regime definition*: how biases get embedded and change. Otherwise 'interaction' reifies regimes as 'billiard balls', each containing 'the principles of its own dynamic' (Bourdieu). Interaction also reshapes regimes from within (human rights actors trying to change trade, and vice versa).

**Trade barriers are constructed.** The common view is that a mandate to liberalise means a structural free-market bias. In fact virtually all government action affects trade (macroeconomic, labour, environmental, health policy), and almost every market-access impediment is attributable to some government action. So liberalisation requires 'the construction of some governmental measures as distortions of trade — and others not'. Three treatments follow: *distortions* face progressive elimination (rounds, prohibitions, dispute settlement); *market-supporting regulation* gets harmonisation, proportionality review, technical assistance, mutual recognition; *background* measures get no scrutiny. The politics lie in these 'principles of vision', 'frameworks of visibility and invisibility'.

**History.** Early GATT focused on border barriers. From the 1970s, with the decline of embedded liberalism, a new economic liberalism and US elites' worry about Japan's hidden barriers, lists of non-tariff barriers grew: product standards, food safety, IP, environment, currency, censorship. Shared diplomatic understandings gave way to *technical expertise* to justify classification.

**Case: telecoms services.** The WTO Reference Paper codified a decade of developed-country liberalisation experience as 'best practice', 'a transfer of know-how'. Over 80 members now commit to it. Telecoms regulators and trade negotiators worked closely (the FCC's Hundt and USTR's Barshefsky). It created 'an alliance between indeterminate legal principles and determinate programmes of regulatory reform', supported by a reform coalition, commercial interests and a sense of inevitability.

**Implications.** Several kinds of expertise (economic, sectoral, legal, commercial 'feel', 'insider' knowledge) form a professional sensibility. The lack of a 'redemptive narrative' may partly result from an international legal sensibility that 'disavows … explicit political choices': politics conducted 'in a technical register'. But contestation is possible: destabilise the self-evidence of what counts as a barrier, stress 'the radical indeterminacy' of expert knowledge, and use peer review, monitoring and dialogue, the very mechanisms that police background norms, with a range of voices beyond experts.
arguments: Regime interaction is politics; so is the internal definition of regimes.
'Trade barrier' is indeterminate: liberalisation constructs distortions and backgrounds.
Principles of vision shifted from border to behind-the-border measures, built by expertise.
Telecoms Reference Paper: expert best practice encoded as law.
Contest regimes by destabilising their principles of vision, including through expertise.
readings.context: Turns the Kennedy 'foreground/background' and expertise themes ([[kennedy-hr-problem]], [[kennedy-chart]]) onto the WTO. Complicates [[bello-wto]] (trade's neutrality) and [[fischer-lescano-teubner]] (regimes as rationalities). Backgrounded measures are the 'local rules' of [[danielsen-local-rules]]. Expert codification parallels [[kingsbury-gal]] and [[miller-parity]]. Fragmentation context: [[ilc-fragmentation-phenomenon]].

readings.author: Martti Koskenniemi
readings.title: The Laws That Rule Us: The Legal Infrastructure of Global Capitalism
readings.summary:
New Left Review 154 (2025), excerpts. Epigraph from Foucault: law 'is born of real battles, victories, massacres and conquests'.

**Anderson's critique.** 'The Standard of Civilization' (NLR 2023): sovereign equality (Charter art. 2(1)) hides hierarchy. Grotius and Vattel drew a line between Europe and the rest; 'civilization' became 'modernization' and 'development'. Following Schmitt, post-1918 law is 'fundamentally discriminatory' (Versailles reparations). Since 1945 American hegemony: Suez, Vietnam, proxy wars, Belgrade 1999, Iraq 2003. Without enforcement law becomes 'no more than opinion', yet it remains 'a major ideological force'.

**Koskenniemi's reply.** Much is right, but there is 'a certain myopia' common to left critiques. It focuses on a criminal-law-oriented, domestic-analogy conception of public international law (Security Council, ICJ, ICC). That is 'the weak part'. Overlooked is 'the legal infrastructure of global capitalism': 'the laws — public and private, domestic and international — that regulate practically all aspects of social life by distributing rights and duties, powers and vulnerabilities'. The forms of the sovereign state, contract and property spread through empire; they are 'neither weak nor manipulable at will'. Not a system or plan, but since the 1980s the taken-for-granted grammar of 'global governance'. 'Globalization has been an intensely legalistic affair.'

**How law works.** Law operates in contestation as claims about what is legally true. It is in play long before compliance: in defining 'interests', who decides, which assets count, whether a relationship is public or private, domestic or international, economic or political. 'Law intrudes everywhere. It does not merely limit and constrain; … it empowers and enables.' 'Property' and 'sovereignty' are 'space-filling' words, each with Hohfeldian correlatives (liability, disability, no-right). Hence 'there is no such thing as "deregulation"': removing a duty empowers someone. Kennedy: capital, labour, credit, money and power 'are creatures of law. Law not only regulates these things, it creates them.'

**Lawyers.** Legality is a creation of legal discourse; lawyers are its 'native speakers'. Look at US law firms, arbitration, the World Bank's lawyers, EU law, Pistor's 'code of capital'. Law's power 'lies in its connotation of objective neutrality': the history of violence is forgotten. The 'politics of law' is the distance between a claim and its consolidation as 'true'; bias emerges as 'some claims begin to win systematically, others to lose'.
arguments: Agrees: public international law serves hegemony and is weakly enforced.
But the left critique targets the weak part and misses the legal infrastructure of capitalism.
Sovereignty, property and contract distribute power globally and are robust.
Law empowers as well as constrains; 'deregulation' is re-regulation.
Lawyers and law's aura of neutrality turn claims into systematic wins and losses.
readings.tldr: Perry Anderson rightly calls public international law an instrument of Western hegemony that is 'neither truthfully international nor genuinely law'. But the left critique targets the *weak* part (UN Charter, ICC, laws of war). It misses the *legal infrastructure of global capitalism*: the public and private, domestic and international rules of sovereignty, property and contract that distribute powers and vulnerabilities everywhere. Law empowers as well as constrains; there is no 'deregulation'. Lawyers are its 'native speakers', and law's power lies in its connotation of neutrality.
readings.context: Koskenniemi's political-economy turn, building on [[cohen-property-sovereignty]] (Hohfeld, property as sovereignty), [[danielsen-local-rules]] and [[iglp-gvc]]. Answers the realist dismissal of law in [[goldsmith-mercer]] and [[nyt-putin-ukraine]]. Civilisation/hierarchy connects to [[anghie-imperialism]], [[becker-lorca-mestizo]] and [[borrell-statement]]. Contrast [[roepke-1955]], who wanted the economy outside politics. Expertise: [[lang-regimes]], [[kennedy-legal-expertise-war]].
